options: a: Move toward the left side of your lane.,b: Avoid driving in the bicycle lane.,c: Signal for 100 feet before turning.
note: Before making a right turn, you should begin signaling well in advance—about 100 feet in most urban areas—so other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians know your intentions. As you slow for the turn, stay close to the right edge, check mirrors and your right blind spot, and yield to pedestrians and bicyclists in the crosswalk or bike lane.

question: When turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street, you must:
options: a: Move into the left lane or to the left side of a single lane.,b: Move into the right lane or to the right side of a single lane.,c: Move into the right lane or to the left side of a single lane.
note: When turning left from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, you should start from the far‑left lane and enter the left lane on the new street, unless signs or lane markings direct otherwise. Staying in the left lane for a left‑to‑left turn keeps traffic organized and reduces conflicts with vehicles going straight or turning right.

question: When preparing to make a left turn from a two-way street, you should drive:
options: a: Near the right-hand side of the road.,b: Near the centerline.,c: On the left of the centerline.
note: On a two‑way street, you prepare for a left turn by moving as close as is safe to the centerline (or into a marked left‑turn lane). This positions you correctly for the turn and keeps the right lane open for through traffic and right‑turning vehicles.

question: When completing a right turn, which lane is the appropriate one to finish in?
options: a: Any lane free of traffic.,b: The lane closest to the left edge of the road.,c: The lane closest to the right edge of the road.
note: To make a right turn, you should end your turn in the lane closest to the right edge of the road. 'Do not swing wide into another lane of traffic.'

question: While a left turn at an intersection is allowed from either of two lanes, a U-turn is permitted from
options: a: Either of the two lanes,b: Only the left lane,c: Any lane that is open
note: A U‑turn is made from the far‑left position because you are turning across oncoming lanes and need the widest turning radius. Use the left‑turn lane or the far‑left lane only, and never start a U‑turn from a center or right lane unless specific signs or markings direct you to do so.

question: To turn right onto a two-way street from another two-way street, begin in the right-hand lane and end in:
options: a: Any lane that is available,b: The left lane,c: The lane closest to the curb
note: When turning right from a two‑way street onto another two‑way street, start in the right‑hand lane and end in the lane closest to the right curb. Do not swing wide into the left lane; staying in the right lane keeps you out of the path of vehicles that may be turning left or going straight in the other lanes.

question: Left turns on red are allowed from:
options: a: From a one-way street onto a two-way street.,b: From a one-way street onto another one-way street.,c: From a two-way street onto a one-way street.
note: In most U.S. states that allow left turns on red, you may turn left on red only from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, after stopping and yielding to traffic and pedestrians. Left turns on red from or onto two‑way streets are generally not allowed unless specifically signed.

question: U-turns are prohibited:
options: a: In a parking lot.,b: On or near any curve or hill.,c: On a straight roadway with a clear view for 500 feet in both directions.
note: You must not make a U‑turn where you cannot see far enough ahead to do it safely. On or near a curve or hill, your view of oncoming traffic is limited, so a U‑turn there is prohibited because approaching drivers may not see you in time to react.

question: You should never make a U-turn.
options: a: In residential districts.,b: At or on a railroad crossing.,c: Where there isn't a ‘No U-turn’ sign posted.
note: You must never make a U‑turn at or on a railroad crossing. Trains cannot stop quickly, and tracks must be kept clear at all times. Even if there is no train in sight, using the crossing area to turn around is unsafe and illegal.

question: U-turns in business districts are:
options: a: Always illegal anywhere in a business district.,b: Legal anywhere in a business district if oncoming vehicles are not a hazard.,c: Legal only at intersections in a business district when not otherwise prohibited and when safe.
note: In many states, U‑turns in business districts are allowed only at intersections, and only when there is no sign prohibiting them and it is safe. Making a U‑turn mid‑block in a business district is typically illegal because of frequent driveways, heavy traffic, and limited space.

question: When on a one-way street, a left turn onto another one-way street is permitted only if:
options: a: You increase your speed before the turn.,b: Traffic on the street moves to the right.,c: Traffic on the street moves to the left.
note: When turning left from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, you may turn into the left‑moving traffic lanes, including on a red light where permitted, after stopping and yielding. This is only allowed when the street you are turning onto carries traffic to the left and there is no sign prohibiting the turn.

question: You are permitted to turn left on a red light only from a:
options: a: One-way street onto a two-way street.,b: One-way street onto a one-way street.,c: Two-way street onto a one-way street.
note: In most U.S. states that allow left turns on red, you may only do so when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after stopping and yielding to traffic, pedestrians, and bicyclists with a green light. Always check for signs that prohibit the turn.

question: When making a left turn from a one-way street onto another one-way street, where should your vehicle be positioned at the start of the turn?
options: a: The lane closest to the center of the street.,b: The far-left lane.,c: You can turn from any lane.
note: When turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street, position your vehicle in the far-left lane before the turn. This lane is closest to the left curb and gives you the correct angle to enter the new street safely and predictably.

question: To turn left from a one-way street with multiple lanes onto a two-way street, start the turn in:
options: a: The far left lane.,b: Any available lane.,c: The lane closest to the middle of the street.
note: When turning left from a one-way street with multiple lanes onto a two-way street, start from the far-left lane. This lane is closest to the left curb and lines you up properly to enter the correct lane on the two-way street while minimizing conflict with other traffic.

question: When making a left turn from a two-way road onto a one-way road, you must:
options: a: Turn into any lane.,b: Turn into first lane.,c: Turn into second lane.
note: When turning left from a two-way road onto a one-way road, you must turn into the first available lane on the one-way street, usually the lane closest to the left curb. Entering the first lane keeps traffic organized and prevents you from cutting across other lanes where vehicles may be traveling.

question: When merging an interstate highway, you must:
options: a: Select a safe gap and merge into the lane of traffic.,b: Merge across two lanes at once.,c: Always stop before entering the highway.
note: When entering a highway, use the acceleration lane to match the speed of traffic, signal, and select a safe gap. Merge smoothly into one lane of traffic without stopping unless it is absolutely necessary for safety.

question: Upon entering a freeway from an on-ramp and merging, your speed should be driving at:
options: a: The legal speed limit on the freeway,b: About the same speed as the freeway traffic,c: About 10 m.p.h. slower than the freeway speed limit
note: When merging onto a freeway, use the on‑ramp to accelerate to about the same speed as vehicles already on the freeway. Being near the speed of traffic allows you to merge smoothly and safely, as long as you do not exceed the posted speed limit.

question: If you are exiting a parking lot, you...
options: a: Must turn either left or right only when it is safe,b: Have the right-of-way,c: Must yield to traffic and pedestrians before re-entering the road
note: When exiting a parking lot or driveway, you must yield to all traffic already on the road and to pedestrians on the sidewalk or crossing the driveway. Do not assume you have the right‑of‑way; wait until there is a safe gap before entering the roadway.

question: Even with a green light, if the intersection is obstructed by traffic, you should...
options: a: Enter the intersection and wait until traffic clears,b: Merge into another lane and try to go around the traffic,c: Stay out of the intersection until traffic clears
note: A green light does not guarantee you can enter the intersection. If traffic ahead is stopped and there is not enough room for your vehicle to completely clear the intersection, you must wait behind the stop line. Blocking an intersection is illegal and can prevent cross traffic from moving.

question: A vehicle that enters a road from a driveway:
options: a: Has the right-of-way,b: Must stop if needed and yield the right-of-way to traffic on the roadway and to pedestrians,c: Must yield only to traffic approaching from the right
note: A driver entering a road from a driveway, alley, or parking lot must stop if necessary and yield to all vehicles already on the roadway and to pedestrians on the sidewalk or crossing the driveway. Traffic already on the road has the right‑of‑way in this situation.

question: You are driving on the freeway and need to exit. You should:
options: a: Use your turn signal, check traffic, and move safely into the exit lane in advance of your exit.,b: Exit immediately without signaling if you see your exit at the last moment.,c: Accelerate sharply into the exit lane to avoid missing your exit.,d: None of the above
note: To exit a freeway safely, you should plan ahead, signal, and move into the exit lane when it is safe. Signal and check mirrors and blind spots as you change lanes one at a time. Once in the proper lane, maintain a safe speed and continue signaling as you approach and take the exit. Never exit suddenly or without signaling.

question: You missed your exit on the freeway. You should not:
options: a: Continue on the freeway and find an alternate route to your destination.,b: Proceed to the next exit.,c: Back up on the road or shoulder.
note: If you miss your freeway exit, you must never back up on the freeway or on the shoulder because it is extremely dangerous and illegal. Instead, continue to the next exit or follow the freeway until you can safely leave and re-route to your destination.

question: You want to enter the freeway but you don't see a gap in traffic. You should:
options: a: Maintain your speed and force other drivers to create a gap.,b: Adjust your speed on the ramp so you can merge into a safe gap in traffic, avoiding a stop unless absolutely necessary.,c: Stop at the end of the ramp and wait there for a gap in freeway traffic.
note: When entering a freeway, you should use the on‑ramp and acceleration lane to reach the speed of traffic and merge when there is a safe gap. If you do not see a gap, you may need to adjust your speed on the ramp, but you should avoid stopping at the end of the ramp unless absolutely necessary, because stopped vehicles are harder for fast traffic to avoid.

question: You want to enter a gap in highway traffic. You should:
options: a: Watch only the vehicles behind the gap.,b: Check traffic behind and beside you using your mirrors and by looking over your shoulder before merging.,c: Speed up and rely on other vehicles to make way for you.
note: To enter a gap in highway traffic safely, you must know what is happening both in front of you and behind you. Check your mirrors and look over your shoulder to check your blind spot before merging. Watching only the vehicles behind the gap or trying to force others to move by speeding up is unsafe.

question: When merging onto the highway, find a gap in the closest lane, accelerate to match the flow of traffic, signal your intention, and:
options: a: Expect traffic to allow you to proceed into the lane,b: Merge carefully into the gap.,c: Wait for the lane to clear before merging.
note: When merging, you should identify a safe gap in the nearest lane, signal, accelerate to match the flow of traffic, and then merge smoothly into that gap. Do not assume other drivers will yield for you; it is your responsibility to merge only when it is safe.

question: When entering into traffic from a parked position:
options: a: Should drive more slowly than other traffic for 200 feet.,b: Should wait for a large enough gap to get up to the speed of traffic.,c: Should wait for the first two vehicles to pass
note: When pulling out from a parked or stopped position, signal and wait for a gap large enough to let you accelerate up to the speed of traffic without forcing other drivers to brake suddenly. Entering too slowly or cutting in front of close traffic can create a hazard.

question: Before merging onto the freeway, check traffic on the freeway by:
options: a: Using your rearview and side mirrors.,b: Using your rearview mirror.,c: Using your side mirror and looking over your shoulder.
note: Before merging onto a freeway, use your mirrors to check traffic and then look over your shoulder to check your blind spot in the lane you plan to enter. This combination of mirrors and a quick head check helps ensure there is no vehicle hidden alongside you before you merge.

question: As you approach your exit on the highway, when should you begin to slow down?
options: a: About halfway through the deceleration lane.,b: As you approach the deceleration lane.,c: Immediately upon entering the deceleration lane.
note: Use the deceleration lane to slow down, not the main travel lane. Maintain highway speed until you reach the deceleration lane, then reduce speed promptly and smoothly after you are in that lane so you do not disrupt through traffic.

question: You've been parked, signaling your intention to merge back into traffic, but have been waiting for a considerable period. Traffic volume is high. What should you do?
options: a: Continue waiting and yielding to traffic in the lane.,b: Slowly inch your vehicle into the traffic lane.,c: Drive on the shoulder until a gap in traffic appears.
note: When entering traffic from a parked or stopped position, you must yield to vehicles already moving in the lane. Wait until there is a large enough gap to signal, pull out, and accelerate to the speed of traffic. Do not force your way in or drive on the shoulder.

question: If the light is green but the intersection is blocked by other vehicles, how should you proceed?
options: a: Partially enter the intersection as allowed by traffic.,b: Wait and do not enter the intersection until your vehicle can get completely across.,c: Drive around the traffic on the shoulder to help ease the congestion.
note: A green light does not give you the right to block an intersection. You may only enter when there is enough space for your vehicle to clear completely. If traffic ahead is stopped and would trap you in the intersection, wait behind the stop line until you can get all the way through.

question: You must not pass another vehicle:
options: a: On a multi-lane one-way street,b: Where someone is likely to enter or cross the road,c: When a broken yellow line is on the left side of your lane
note: You must not pass where other road users are likely to enter or cross, such as at intersections, driveways, and crosswalks, because another vehicle, pedestrian, or cyclist may appear suddenly. Passing is allowed on multi‑lane one‑way streets and when a broken yellow line is on your side, as long as it is otherwise safe and legal.

question: When a vehicle approaching you initiates a left turn:
options: a: Maintain your speed and take your right of way,b: Honk your horn to warn the driver and maintain your speed,c: Slow or stop to prevent a collision
note: Even if you have the right‑of‑way, you must do whatever you reasonably can to avoid a collision. If an oncoming driver begins a left turn across your path, be prepared to slow or stop to prevent a crash, because right‑of‑way rules do not protect you from careless or mistaken drivers.

question: When you intend to pass a vehicle on the road, you must...
options: a: Wait until you can see the entire vehicle in your rearview mirror before merging back into your lane,b: Use your horn to alert the other driver of your intention to pass,c: Pass only if there is enough space in the lane ahead of the vehicle,d: None of the above
note: When passing, you must have enough clear space ahead to complete the pass and return safely, and you should not move back into your original lane until you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror. This ensures you are not cutting too closely in front of the other driver and reduces the risk of a rear‑end collision.

question: Once you've passed a vehicle traveling in your direction, it's allowed to return to the right lane:
options: a: After about three seconds.,b: When you can no longer see the passed vehicle over your right shoulder.,c: When you can see the entire front of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.
note: After passing, you should not return to the right lane until you can see the entire front of the vehicle you passed in your rearview mirror. This visual check confirms you have enough space ahead of the other vehicle and will not force that driver to brake suddenly when you move back into the lane.

question: When approaching the top of a hill, you should:
options: a: Speed up slightly.,b: Prepare to stop.,c: Maintain a steady, safe speed and be ready to slow or stop if needed.
note: As you approach the top of a hill, you should maintain a safe, steady speed and be prepared for hazards you cannot yet see, such as stopped traffic, slow vehicles, or pedestrians. You should not speed up, and you generally do not stop unless there is a specific hazard or traffic control requiring it. The key is to control your speed and be ready to react safely.

question: It is illegal to:
options: a: Pass another vehicle in any marked no passing zone.,b: Pass another vehicle over a railroad crossing.,c: Both of the above.
note: Passing is illegal both in a marked no‑passing zone and at or over a railroad crossing. No‑passing zones are marked with solid yellow lines or signs, and you must stay in your lane there. You also may not pass when approaching or on a railroad crossing, typically within about 100 feet, because trains cannot stop quickly and your view of the tracks or oncoming traffic may be limited.

question: When passing on a two-lane road, you should:
options: a: Sound your horn as you pass.,b: Flash your headlights as you pass.,c: Judge the distance to any oncoming vehicles.
note: Before passing on a two‑lane road, you must be sure there is enough clear distance ahead to complete the pass safely. That means carefully judging how far away oncoming vehicles are and how fast they are approaching. If you cannot clearly see enough open road ahead—such as near hills, curves, or other obstructions—you must not start to pass.

question: When passing another vehicle:
options: a: Pass the vehicle as slowly as possible.,b: Drive at the same speed as the vehicle you are passing.,c: Pass the vehicle as safely and as quickly as possible.
note: When you decide to pass, you should move into the passing lane, increase your speed within the legal limit, and complete the pass promptly. Lingering beside another vehicle is unsafe because it increases your time in the opposing lane and in the other driver’s blind spot. Passing should always be done as quickly as is safe and legal, never slowly or at the same speed as the vehicle you are overtaking.

question: Under what legal circumstances can a vehicle leave the roadway to overtake another?
options: a: If the vehicle ahead is turning left.,b: It is not legal under any conditions.,c: If there are two or more one-way lanes.
note: You must stay on the paved or main‑traveled portion of the roadway when passing. It is illegal to drive onto the shoulder, dirt, or any area off the roadway to overtake another vehicle, even if the vehicle ahead is turning left. Passing must be done only within marked lanes on the roadway where it is permitted and safe.

question: When being passed in a no-passing zone, you must:
options: a: Pull off the road.,b: Maintain your speed and position.,c: Slow down and let the other driver safely return to the drive lane.
note: When another driver begins to pass you, even in a no‑passing zone, you must not speed up or change your lane position. Maintain a steady speed and stay in your lane so the passing driver can judge distance and return safely. You may gently reduce speed if needed for safety, but you should not pull off the road or make sudden moves.

question: When passing, return to the right lane if:
options: a: You are one vehicle length ahead of the passed vehicle.,b: You can see both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.,c: You are 50 feet ahead of the passed vehicle.
note: After passing another vehicle, do not move back into the right lane until you can see both of the passed vehicle’s headlights in your inside rearview mirror. This ensures you have enough space ahead of that vehicle and reduces the risk of cutting them off or forcing them to brake suddenly.

question: What's the correct way to parallel park?
options: a: Drive forward into the space without stopping.,b: Stop next to the vehicle behind the open space and then drive forward into the space.,c: Stop next to the vehicle in front of the open space and then back into the space.
note: For standard parallel parking, you first pull up alongside the vehicle in front of the open space, aligning your rear bumpers. Then you back slowly into the space while turning the wheel as directed, adjusting until you are parallel and centered in the space. You do not drive straight forward into a parallel space from the traffic lane.

question: Whould you do when parking your vehicle on a hill?
options: a: Turn your front wheels so the vehicle will roll into the curb or away from traffic if the brakes fail.,b: Make sure your vehicle is left in the 'neutral' position.,c: Make sure your vehicle is in the 'park' position or in gear.
note: When parking on a hill, always secure the vehicle so it cannot roll. Set the parking brake firmly and leave the transmission in Park (for automatic) or in a gear (for manual). In addition, you should turn the front wheels so that if the vehicle does roll, it will roll into the curb or away from traffic, not straight down the hill.

question: To back your vehicle safely, you must not…
options: a: Tap your horn before backing up,b: Check in front and behind your vehicle before you get in,c: Look over your right shoulder as you back up
note: You should never rely on tapping your horn as a primary safety step when backing. Safe backing requires checking both in front of and behind your vehicle before you get in, then looking over your right shoulder and using your mirrors while backing slowly. Sounding the horn is not a standard or required step in normal backing and can give a false sense of safety; the key is thorough observation, not noise.

question: During parallel parking:
options: a: Front wheels are turned toward the street,b: Vehicle is in line with other parked vehicles,c: Rear wheels are touching the curb
note: Parallel parking means your vehicle is parked parallel to the curb and in line with other parked vehicles. Your wheels should generally be straight and your car should not be sticking out into traffic or angled toward the street. The rear wheels should be close to, but not touching, the curb.

question: You are parking your vehicle on a hill. You should:
options: a: Leave the vehicle in neutral,b: Set the parking brake,c: Set the parking brake and leave the vehicle in park
note: When parking on a hill, you should always secure the vehicle by setting the parking brake and placing the transmission in park (or in gear for a manual). This prevents the vehicle from rolling if the brakes fail or if it is bumped. Never leave a parked vehicle on a hill in neutral.

question: Backing a vehicle is:
options: a: Always dangerous to do.,b: Dangerous if you have a helper.,c: Only dangerous in large vehicles.
note: Backing is always a potentially dangerous maneuver because your view is limited and other road users may be in your blind spots. Treat backing as a high‑risk action: check behind your vehicle before getting in, look over your right shoulder, use your mirrors, back slowly, and avoid unnecessary backing whenever possible. Even in small vehicles or with a helper, you must assume extra risk exists and use great caution.

question: If you're parallel parking downhill:
options: a: Turn your wheels sharply toward the side of the road.,b: Turn your wheels away from the side of the road.,c: Keep your wheels straight.
note: When you park facing downhill, turn your front wheels toward the curb or toward the side of the road. If the vehicle rolls, the front tire will contact the curb or shoulder and stop the car from rolling into traffic. Always set the parking brake as well.

question: When you are backing up your vehicle:
options: a: Look through the rear window while backing and check over your shoulder.,b: Press hard on the gas pedal.,c: Rely only on your rearview mirror.
note: When backing up, you should primarily look over your right shoulder through the rear window so you can clearly see the path behind you. Use your mirrors only as helpers, not your main view, and back up slowly using the brake, not the gas, so you can stop quickly if a person, vehicle, or object appears.

question: While parking your car parallel to the curb on a flat road:
options: a: Your front wheels must be turned toward the street.,b: Your wheels must be within 18 inches of the curb.,c: One of your rear wheels must touch the curb.
note: According to most state rules, when parallel parked your wheels must be close to the curb, typically within about 12–18 inches. This keeps your vehicle out of the traffic lane while avoiding contact with the curb.

question: When parking uphill on a two-way street without a curb, your front wheels should be...
options: a: Turn the front wheels to the left toward the center of the road.,b: Turn the front wheels to the right toward the side of the road.,c: Keep the front wheels parallel with the pavement.,d: Turn the wheels toward the curb (only applies when there is a curb).
note: On a hill with no curb, you always want the car to roll away from traffic if the brakes fail. When parking uphill on a two-way street without a curb, turn the front wheels to the right, toward the edge of the road. If the vehicle rolls, it will move off the roadway instead of into the traffic lane.

question: If you park facing uphill on a street with a curb, set the parking brake and:
options: a: Turn the front wheels toward the curb.,b: Turn the front wheels away from the curb.,c: Leave the front wheels straight.
note: When you park facing uphill with a curb, turn the front wheels away from the curb and let the vehicle roll back gently until the tire rests against the curb. If the brakes fail, the curb will stop the car from rolling into traffic.

question: When should your car's front wheels NOT be pointed directly forward?
options: a: When waiting to make a left turn at a traffic light.,b: When parked on a hill or sloping driveway.,c: When parked on the side of a level roadway where there is no curb.
note: Your front wheels should NOT be pointed straight ahead when you are parked on a hill or sloping driveway. On any slope, you must turn the wheels so that if the vehicle starts to roll, it will move away from traffic and not into the street. At a left turn at a traffic light, you should keep the wheels straight until you actually begin the turn, so you are not pushed into oncoming traffic if hit from behind.

question: To park downhill next to a curb, in which direction should you angle your front wheels?
options: a: Into the curb,b: Away from the curb,c: Parallel to the curb
note: When parking downhill next to a curb, turn your front wheels into the curb. If the brakes fail, the car will roll forward and the front tire will rest against the curb, stopping the vehicle from rolling into the traffic lane.

question: Who of the following can park at a blue curb?
options: a: Someone who is either picking up or dropping off passengers at this location.,b: A person who is disabled and has a special placard or vehicle license plate for disabled persons.,c: A person who will only be parked at the curb for less than 15 minutes.
note: A blue curb marks parking reserved for a person with a disability who has a valid disabled placard or special license plates, or for someone driving that person. Others may not park there, even briefly, unless they are transporting a person with a disability and displaying the proper placard or plates.

question: What curb color indicates no stopping or parking allowed?
options: a: Yellow.,b: Red.,c: White.
note: A red curb means you may not stop, stand, or park there at any time, except when required to obey a traffic control device or officer. Red is used to keep areas completely clear for safety or traffic flow.

question: You may not 'double park'
options: a: At any time,b: Except when making a delivery,c: Except while waiting in the vehicle
note: Double parking means stopping or parking alongside a vehicle already parked at the curb. This blocks traffic and can trap the parked vehicle, so it is not allowed at any time, even if you stay in the car or are making a delivery.

question: Parking is never permitted
options: a: In a tunnel,b: On the road side of a parked vehicle,c: All of the above
note: Parking is never allowed in a tunnel or on the road side of a parked vehicle (double parking). Tunnels are confined spaces where stopped vehicles create serious hazards, and double parking blocks traffic and visibility. Because both locations are prohibited, the correct choice is “All of the above.”

question: A blue-painted curb implies parking is:
options: a: Allowed for no longer than 15 minutes.,b: Only allowed when picking up or dropping off passengers.,c: For disabled persons with a special placard or plate.
note: A blue curb marks parking reserved for people with disabilities who display a valid disabled placard or license plate. Others may not park there, even briefly, because these spaces must remain available for drivers and passengers with mobility needs.

question: A red-painted curb indicates:
options: a: Loading zone.,b: The area is reserved for picking up or dropping off passengers.,c: No parking
note: A red curb means no stopping, standing, or parking at any time, except when required by traffic signals or officers. You may not use a red curb as a loading zone or for quick passenger drop‑off; the area must stay clear.

question: A white curb signifies:
options: a: Loading zone for freight or passengers.,b: Loading zone for passengers or mail only.,c: Loading zone for freight only.
note: A white curb means you may stop only long enough to pick up or drop off passengers or mail. You cannot use a white curb as a general loading zone for freight or long-term parking. Freight loading is typically associated with yellow curbs, not white.

question: When an emergency necessitates stopping on a highway, you should:
options: a: Sound your horn at passing cars to get their attention.,b: Get out of your vehicle and flag down the first vehicle that passes.,c: Pull off the road
note: If you must stop on a highway or freeway, you should pull completely off the road and onto the shoulder, well out of moving traffic. Stay in your vehicle with doors locked and seat belt fastened while you wait for help, unless it is unsafe to do so.

question: Parking your vehicle is against the law:
options: a: In an unmarked crosswalk.,b: Within three feet of a private driveway.,c: In a bicycle lane.
note: You may not park in a crosswalk, whether it is marked with painted lines or unmarked at an intersection. Crosswalks must be kept clear so pedestrians can cross safely and drivers have a clear view of them.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A steady yellow arrow traffic light indicates:
options: a: You should speed up so you can make the turn before the light changes.,b: You do not need to signal to turn from the indicated lane.,c: You should prepare to stop and yield the right-of-way to oncoming traffic.
note: A steady yellow arrow means the protected turning phase is ending and the signal will change soon. You should prepare to stop and yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. If you are already in the intersection and cannot stop safely, complete your turn with caution.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A solid red arrow light on a traffic signal signifies:
options: a: Drivers cannot turn in the indicated direction.,b: Drivers may turn in the indicated direction after coming to a complete stop.,c: Drivers may turn in the indicated direction.
note: A solid red arrow means you must stop and you are not allowed to turn in the direction the arrow is pointing. You must remain stopped until the signal changes to green or a green arrow appears.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A solid yellow traffic light indicates the signal is preparing to turn red. If you've entered the intersection on a green light and it turns yellow, you should:
options: a: Stop.,b: Continue moving and clear the intersection safely.,c: Increase your speed so as not to cause an accident.
note: A solid yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red. If you are already in the intersection or so close that stopping might be unsafe, you should continue through and clear the intersection carefully. If you have not yet entered and can stop safely, you must stop.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do before stopping your vehicle at a traffic signal?
options: a: Press down hard on the accelerator.,b: Check your mirrors for surrounding traffic.,c: Set the parking brake.
note: Before stopping at a traffic signal or sign, you should check your mirrors so you know where vehicles are behind and beside you. This helps you brake smoothly and early, reducing the risk of being rear‑ended and allowing you to adjust if another driver is following too closely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A left turn on red traffic light is allowed after a complete stop, but only if:
options: a: You are traveling on a two-way street and turning onto a two-way street.,b: You are traveling on a one-way street and turning onto another one-way street.,c: You yield to all other traffic at the intersection.
note: In many U.S. states, you may turn left on a red light only when turning from a one‑way street onto another one‑way street, after coming to a complete stop and yielding to traffic and pedestrians. Left turns on red are not allowed from a two‑way street onto a two‑way street.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A yellow left arrow on a traffic signal means what?
options: a: Drivers should prepare to yield to oncoming traffic.,b: The protected left turn is about to end.,c: Both of the above.
note: A yellow left arrow means the protected left‑turn phase is ending. Drivers with the yellow arrow should prepare to stop if they can safely do so, and they must be ready to yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians once the signal changes.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: How do red arrow traffic signals differ from regular solid red lights?
options: a: Red arrows are only used to stop traffic which is turning.,b: Red arrows are only used for protected turn lanes.,c: You cannot turn on a red arrow
note: A solid red light means stop, but in many states you may turn right (and sometimes left from a one‑way to a one‑way) after stopping if it is safe and not prohibited by a sign. A red arrow specifically controls the movement in the direction of the arrow and means you must stop and you may not turn in that direction until a green light or green arrow appears.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: At a flashing red traffic signal, you are required to:
options: a: Come to a complete stop,b: Reduce your speed and proceed with caution.,c: Come to a complete stop and remain stopped as long as the light is red.
note: A flashing red light is treated like a stop sign. You must come to a complete stop, then proceed only when it is safe and after yielding to any traffic or pedestrians with the right‑of‑way. You do not have to remain stopped the entire time it is flashing, only until it is safe to go.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: As you near an intersection at the speed limit and the traffic light changes to yellow, you must:
options: a: Slow down and proceed through the intersection without caution.,b: Speed up to cross the intersection before the light turns red.,c: Stop before entering the intersection, unless you are too close to stop safely, in which case proceed with caution
note: A steady yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red. You must stop before entering the intersection if you can do so safely. If you are so close that stopping would be unsafe (for example, you would have to brake very hard and might be hit from behind), you should continue carefully through the intersection instead of stopping abruptly.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You must stop your vehicle:
options: a: At any intersection where a police officer orders you to stop.,b: Where there is a red traffic light.,c: Both of the above.
note: You must always obey a red traffic signal by stopping before the limit line, crosswalk, or intersection. You also must obey lawful orders from a police officer directing traffic, even if those directions differ from the normal signal indications. If an officer tells you to stop, you must stop, regardless of the signal.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When is it safe to proceed through an intersection displaying a steady green light?
options: a: when you can go around the traffic already in the intersection,b: when you have enough space to cross the intersection before the light turns red,c: when you cannot completely cross the intersection
note: A green light means you may go straight or turn, if it is not prohibited, but only when the intersection is clear and it is safe. You must not enter the intersection unless there is enough space for your vehicle to completely clear it without blocking cross traffic when the light changes.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A flashing yellow light at a crossing indicates:
options: a: You should treat the signal like a stop sign.,b: Stop. Yield to all cross traffic before crossing in the intersection.,c: Slow down and be alert at the upcoming intersection.
note: A flashing yellow light means proceed with caution. You do not have to stop, but you must slow down, look carefully in all directions, and be prepared to yield to pedestrians and cross traffic if needed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A solid green traffic light at an intersection means:
options: a: Increase your speed.,b: Adjust your mirrors.,c: You may proceed through the intersection or turn, if it is safe and you yield to pedestrians and traffic already in the intersection.
note: A solid green light means you may go straight or turn, if it is safe and you are not facing signs or signals that prohibit the movement. You must still yield to pedestrians in crosswalks and to any vehicles or bicyclists already in the intersection, and only proceed at a safe, reasonable speed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When facing a red light displaying a green arrow, you are permitted to turn in the direction of the arrow *only if*:
options: a: You first come to a complete stop.,b: You wait until the light changes.,c: You are in the proper lane, the roadway is clear, and you yield to pedestrians and any traffic already in the intersection.
note: A green arrow means you have a protected turn in the direction of the arrow. Oncoming traffic has a red light, but you must still be in the correct lane for that turn and yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, and any vehicles already in the intersection before proceeding.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You cannot legally enter an intersection if:
options: a: You cannot get all the way across and clear the intersection before the light turns red.,b: The light is flashing yellow and you didn't stop first.,c: The light is yellow and you cannot stop safely.
note: You must not enter an intersection if your vehicle cannot clear it completely before the light turns red. Blocking the intersection can prevent cross traffic from moving and is illegal in many jurisdictions, even if the light was green or yellow when you entered.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: For a green arrow, you must:
options: a: Yield to pedestrians and any vehicles or bicyclists already in the intersection.,b: Yield to pedestrians only in the intersection.,c: Wait four seconds before proceeding.
note: A green arrow gives you a protected turn in the direction of the arrow, but you must still yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk and to any vehicles or bicyclists already in the intersection. Do not wait an arbitrary amount of time; proceed as soon as it is safe and lawful to do so.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When approaching a non-functioning traffic light, what should the driver do?
options: a: Come to a full stop, then yield the right-of-way and proceed cautiously when it is safe.,b: If the intersection is clear, you may proceed without stopping.,c: Drive quickly through the intersection to get out of the way of other vehicles.
note: When a traffic signal is not working, treat the intersection as an all-way stop. Come to a complete stop at the limit line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection, then yield the right-of-way and proceed only when it is safe. Never speed through a dark signal.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If your traffic signal turns green, but a pedestrian is still in the crosswalk after the "DON'T WALK" signal is flashing, what should you do?
options: a: Wait until the pedestrian is out of your path and it is safe before proceeding.,b: Wait until the pedestrian signals that it is okay for you to proceed.,c: Wait until the pedestrian has crossed the street completely before proceeding.
note: Drivers must always yield to pedestrians who are still in the crosswalk, even if the pedestrian signal is flashing “DON’T WALK” and your light is green. You may proceed once the pedestrian is out of your path and you can pass safely, even if they are still in another lane of the crosswalk.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: At a corner with a stop sign, you are required to come to a complete stop:
options: a: After crossing the crosswalk,b: Out far enough to see cross traffic,c: In back of the crosswalk
note: At a stop sign with a marked crosswalk, you must stop before the crosswalk or limit line. Stopping behind the crosswalk protects pedestrians and keeps the crossing clear. If you need a better view after stopping, you may then move forward slowly and stop again if necessary.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When approaching a stop sign at an intersection, you are required to:
options: a: Stop and check for traffic before proceeding,b: Slow down and yield to cross traffic,c: Proceed with caution without stopping,d: None of the above
note: At a stop sign, you must come to a complete stop at the limit line, before the crosswalk, or before entering the intersection. After stopping, look for traffic and pedestrians in all directions and proceed only when it is safe.

question: Traffic signs with a blue background provide details about:
options: a: Motorist services.,b: Construction and maintenance.,c: Mileage information.
note: Blue traffic signs are used for motorist services and information, such as rest areas, gas, food, lodging, hospitals, and other driver services. They do not indicate rules you must obey; those are usually shown on white rectangular regulatory signs.

question: Signs with orange backgrounds indicate:
options: a: General warning signs.,b: Construction and maintenance warning signs.,c: Regulatory signs.
note: Orange traffic signs are used for construction and maintenance warning signs. They alert drivers to road work, lane closures, detours, and other temporary conditions in work zones so you can slow down and proceed with extra caution.

question: Signs for construction and maintenance zones:
options: a: Have a red background with green writing.,b: Have an orange background with black writing.,c: Have a yellow background with blue writing.
note: Construction and maintenance zone signs are typically orange with black writing or symbols. The bright orange color warns drivers of temporary work areas so they can reduce speed, watch for workers and equipment, and follow any changed traffic patterns.

question: Traffic control devices used in construction and maintenance zones are colored:
options: a: Red.,b: Orange.,c: Yellow.
note: Traffic control devices in construction and maintenance zones—such as cones, barrels, barricades, and many work-zone signs—are usually orange. This color signals a temporary work area so drivers know to slow down, stay alert, and follow posted directions.

question: What's the shape of a railroad crossing warning sign?
options: a: Pentagon.,b: Round.,c: Crossbuck.
note: The advance warning sign for a railroad crossing is a round (circular) yellow sign with a black X and the letters “RR.” The crossbuck (X-shaped) sign is posted at the actual crossing itself, but when asked for the shape of the railroad crossing warning sign, the correct answer is the round warning sign.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A traffic sign featuring a red circle with a slash through a symbol indicates...
options: a: The maneuver shown by the symbol is not allowed,b: The maneuver shown on the sign should be executed with extreme caution,c: Do not drive faster than the posted speed limit
note: A red circle with a diagonal slash over a symbol is a universal "prohibition" sign. Whatever action is shown inside the circle is not allowed—for example, no U‑turn, no left turn, or no parking. Drivers must not perform the maneuver shown.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Typically, the first sign for drivers nearing a highway-rail crossing is...
options: a: A crossbuck sign,b: A speed limit sign,c: An advance warning sign
note: For most highway‑rail crossings, the first sign you see in advance is a round, yellow railroad advance warning sign placed before the tracks. The crossbuck (white X) is located at the actual crossing, not as the first advance sign. Drivers should recognize the round advance warning sign as the early alert to slow, look, and listen for trains.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A diamond-shaped sign implies:
options: a: Yield.,b: Stop.,c: Warning.
note: Diamond‑shaped signs are warning signs. They alert drivers to special road conditions or hazards ahead, such as curves, merging traffic, or pedestrian crossings, so you can slow down and proceed with caution.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A pentagon-shaped sign is a:
options: a: Stop sign.,b: Regulatory sign.,c: School zone or school crossing sign.
note: A pentagon (five‑sided) sign indicates a school zone or school crossing. When you see this shape, watch for children, reduce speed as required, and be prepared to stop for pedestrians in or near the roadway.

question: Construction zone signs typically are:
options: a: Square or rectangular with white and red coloring.,b: Round or octagonal with black and yellow coloring.,c: Diamond-shaped or rectangular with orange and black coloring.
note: Construction and maintenance warning signs are usually diamond‑shaped or rectangular and use an orange background with black symbols or lettering. These signs alert you to road work, lane shifts, workers, and equipment so you can slow down and drive carefully through the work zone.

question: Regulatory signs are colored:
options: a: Green.,b: Yellow.,c: White.
note: Regulatory signs that tell you what you must or must not do (such as speed limit, no parking, one way) are typically white with black or red lettering or symbols. The white background indicates a law or regulation that you are required to obey.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When you encounter a pedestrian using a motorized wheelchair in a crosswalk at an intersection, what should you do?
options: a: Remain stopped behind the crosswalk line until the motorized wheelchair has safely finished crossing.,b: Remain stopped behind the nearest crosswalk line until the motorized wheelchair is beyond the range of your vehicle.,c: Assume right-of-way if the motorized wheelchair stops in the crosswalk.
note: Pedestrians, including those using motorized wheelchairs, have the right‑of‑way in crosswalks. You must remain stopped behind the nearest crosswalk line until the person is safely beyond the path your vehicle could take, not just until they are technically out of the painted crosswalk. This ensures you do not endanger them if you turn or move forward.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When approaching an intersection without Stop or Yield signs, you are required to...
options: a: Yield to traffic and pedestrians already in the intersection,b: Yield to the vehicle on your right if it reaches the intersection at the same time as you,c: All of the above
note: At an intersection without Stop or Yield signs, you must yield to traffic and pedestrians already in the intersection and also yield to the vehicle on your right if you arrive at the same time. Both rules apply, so “All of the above” is correct.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If two vehicles arrive simultaneously at a four-way stop, what determines who proceeds first?
options: a: The driver on the right yields to the driver on the left,b: The driver on the left yields to the driver on the right,c: The first vehicle to reach the intersection must yield
note: At a four‑way stop where two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left must yield to the driver on the right. The vehicle on the right proceeds first, which helps avoid confusion and collisions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: At an unmarked T-intersection, you are required to yield to:
options: a: Traffic on the road you are entering,b: Traffic on the road you are leaving,c: Pedestrians in the crosswalk,d: None of the above
note: At an unmarked T‑intersection, the traffic on the through road (the road that continues straight) has the right‑of‑way. The driver on the terminating road must yield to traffic on the road being entered. You must also yield to any pedestrians crossing, whether or not a crosswalk is marked.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: At intersections, crosswalks, and railroad crossings, you must:
options: a: Stop,b: Look to the sides of your vehicle to see what is coming.,c: Slowly pass vehicles that seem to be stopped for no reason.
note: At intersections, crosswalks, and railroad crossings, you must actively look to the sides to see what is coming. You should scan left, right, and ahead so you can slow or stop if needed. You are not required to stop every time, only when conditions or signs/signals require it.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a pedestrian is crossing your lane where there isn't a designated crosswalk, you should:
options: a: Make sure the pedestrian can see you before proceeding.,b: Cautiously drive around the pedestrian.,c: Stop and let the pedestrian finish crossing.
note: Pedestrians always have the right-of-way, even in unmarked crosswalks. 'Before entering an intersection, look left, right, and ahead to check for vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians. Be prepared to slow down and stop if necessary. Pedestrians always have the right-of-way.'

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You want to make a right turn at the corner. A pedestrian with a guide dog is at the corner ready to cross the street in front of you. Before making your right turn, you should:
options: a: Turn off your engine until the person crosses the street.,b: Tell the pedestrian when to cross the street.,c: Wait until the person crosses the street.
note: When a pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane is crossing or about to cross in front of you, you must wait until the person has completely crossed and is safely out of your path. Blind or visually impaired pedestrians have the right-of-way, and you must not start your turn until they are clear.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When stopped at an intersection and intending to turn left, what actions should a driver take?
options: a: Turn immediately if there are no pedestrians.,b: Take the right-of-way turn before oncoming traffic.,c: Give the right-of-way to any approaching vehicle that is close enough to be dangerous.
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians in the crosswalk. If an approaching vehicle is close enough to pose a danger, you must wait and give it the right‑of‑way before completing your turn.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: It is illegal to enter an intersection or crosswalk when:
options: a: The light is yellow,b: The light is flashing red,c: You cannot cross without obstructing traffic from either side.
note: You must not enter an intersection or crosswalk unless there is enough space for your vehicle to completely clear it without blocking cross traffic, even if the light is green. Entering when you will obstruct traffic is illegal and unsafe.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If a vehicle in front of you has stopped at a crosswalk, you must...
options: a: Change lanes, look carefully, and pass,b: Tap your horn to let the driver know you are waiting,c: Stop and proceed only when you are sure the crosswalk is clear and it is safe
note: If a vehicle has stopped at a crosswalk, you must also stop and not pass that vehicle. A stopped vehicle may be yielding to a pedestrian you cannot see. Remain stopped until you are sure the crosswalk is clear and it is safe to proceed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You want to turn left at an intersection ahead. A car reaches the intersection from the opposite direction and moves straight ahead. You
options: a: Must wait for the car to go through before you turn,b: May enter the intersection to prepare for your left turn if the light is green and it is safe,c: Can turn left. You have the right-of-way
note: When you are turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic that is going straight or turning right. If a car coming from the opposite direction is going straight through the intersection, you must wait and let it pass before you make your left turn.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Upon arriving at an intersection, a driver...
options: a: Must yield the right-of-way to traffic already in the intersection,b: Has the right-of-way over traffic already in the intersection,c: Must drive straight through the intersection even if another vehicle is already in the intersection
note: A driver approaching an intersection must yield to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection. Traffic that is already in the intersection has the right‑of‑way, so you must wait until it is clear before proceeding.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You should not start across an intersection if you know you will...
options: a: Block the intersection when the light turns red.,b: Unless you enter the intersection on a yellow light.,c: Unless you enter the intersection on a green light.,d: None of the above
note: You must not enter an intersection unless you are sure there is enough space to clear it completely. If you enter and then have to stop in the intersection when the light turns red, you are illegally blocking cross traffic and can cause congestion and collisions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You may not block an intersection during rush hour:
options: a: Unless you entered the intersection on a green light.,b: Under any circumstances,c: Unless you have the right-of-way or a green light.
note: You may only enter an intersection if there is enough space on the other side for your vehicle, even during rush hour. Having a green light or the right‑of‑way does not excuse you from this rule. If traffic is stopped ahead and you cannot clear the intersection, you must wait behind the stop line, even with a green light, so you do not block cross traffic.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do if the driver ahead of you stops at a crosswalk?
options: a: Cautiously pass the vehicle at 10 mph or slower.,b: Stop,c: Change lanes
note: If the driver ahead of you stops at a crosswalk, you must also stop and not pass. There may be a pedestrian in the crosswalk that you cannot see. Passing a stopped vehicle at a crosswalk is dangerous and often illegal because it puts pedestrians directly in your path.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Under what circumstances should you yield your right-of-way?
options: a: Often,b: Whenever it helps prevent collisions.,c: Never. It confuses other drivers.
note: Right‑of‑way rules help traffic flow safely, but you should never insist on your right‑of‑way if it could lead to a collision. If another driver does not yield when they should, it is safer to let them go first. Yielding your right‑of‑way when it helps prevent a crash is both safer and expected.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When turning left at an intersection:
options: a: You should always yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.,b: Oncoming traffic and pedestrians should yield to you.,c: You should never yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians who are in or about to enter the crosswalk. Oncoming vehicles going straight or close enough to be a hazard have the right‑of‑way, and pedestrians crossing your path must be allowed to cross before you turn.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You want to turn left at an upcoming corner. Yield the right-of-way to:
options: a: Oncoming vehicles also turning left.,b: All approaching vehicles that are close enough to be dangerous and any pedestrians crossing your path.,c: Pedestrians on the sidewalk waiting for a "Walk" signal.
note: When turning left, you must yield to all oncoming vehicles that are close enough to be a hazard, whether they are going straight or turning, and to any pedestrians crossing the street you are turning onto. Do not start your turn until you are sure oncoming traffic and pedestrians will not be put in danger.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When approaching the multi-lane roundabout and intending to continue straight ahead, you must...
options: a: Choose either lane (if permitted by signs/markings) and exit in the same lane you entered.,b: Choose the right-hand lane only and exit in the right-hand lane, regardless of signs or markings.,c: Choose the left-hand lane only and exit, regardless of signs or markings.
note: In a typical multi‑lane roundabout, if you are going straight through, you may usually enter from either the left or right lane and should exit in the same lane you used to enter. Always choose your lane based on your intended exit and follow lane markings and signs, which may restrict certain movements from specific lanes.

question: Drivers proceed within the roundabout:
options: a: In a counter-clockwise direction,b: In a clockwise direction,c: In both directions
note: In U.S. roundabouts, all traffic travels in a counter‑clockwise direction around the central island. You enter to the right, circulate counter‑clockwise, and exit to the right. You must not drive clockwise or against the flow of traffic in a roundabout.

question: If a child is about to enter the roadway unexpectedly, you must:
options: a: Immediately slow down and be prepared to stop.,b: Flash your headlights.,c: Sound a sharp blast of your horn.
note: If a child is about to enter the roadway, you must immediately slow down and be prepared to stop. Children are unpredictable and may suddenly run into traffic, so you should reduce speed, cover the brake, and be ready to stop completely if needed. Use the horn only if it will help alert the child without creating more danger.

question: As you get closer to a roundabout, be sure to:
options: a: Increase your speed.,b: Decrease your speed.,c: Maintain your speed.
note: When approaching a roundabout, you must slow down so you have time to observe traffic already in the circle, yield if necessary, and choose the correct gap before entering. Entering too fast makes it harder to yield and increases the risk of a collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Drivers approaching a roundabout must:
options: a: Stop in the middle of the roundabout.,b: Yield to traffic already in the roundabout.,c: Yield to entering traffic.
note: Drivers approaching a roundabout must yield to traffic already in the roundabout. Vehicles inside the circle have the right‑of‑way. You slow or stop before entering if needed, then merge when there is a safe gap. You should never stop in the middle of the roundabout except to avoid a collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a driver observes pedestrians in a crosswalk ahead, what action should they take?
options: a: Continue ahead. The motorist has the right-of-way.,b: Wait for the pedestrians to cross the street.,c: Pull to the right and go around the pedestrians.
note: When pedestrians are in a crosswalk, marked or unmarked, they have the right‑of‑way. You must slow down and stop if necessary, waiting until they have safely crossed your lane before proceeding. Going around pedestrians is unsafe and illegal.

question: If you observe a pedestrian jaywalking, you should:
options: a: Must slow down and stop if necessary to avoid hitting them.,b: Do not have to slow down or stop for them.,c: Should honk your horn at them.
note: Even if a pedestrian is crossing illegally (jaywalking), you must still do everything you can to avoid hitting them. Slow down, be prepared to stop, and stop if needed to let them pass safely. Drivers must always use due care to avoid colliding with pedestrians, regardless of who has the right‑of‑way.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When you encounter a pedestrian with a guide dog or a white cane:
options: a: The pedestrian must yield the right-of-way.,b: You must yield the right-of-way.,c: Honk your horn to let them know you are there.
note: Drivers must always yield the right‑of‑way to pedestrians who are blind or visually impaired and using a white cane or guide dog. These pedestrians may not be able to see or hear your vehicle, so you must stop or slow as needed and never honk or try to force them to hurry.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Pedestrians crossing at corners have the right-of-way:
options: a: Only at controlled intersections.,b: Only when a crosswalk is painted on the street.,c: Whether or not a crosswalk is marked.
note: At intersections and corners, the area where pedestrians cross is considered a crosswalk whether or not it is painted. Pedestrians have the right‑of‑way in both marked and unmarked crosswalks, so drivers must yield to them when they are crossing at corners.

question: You are driving on the freeway. The vehicle in front of you is a large truck. You should drive
options: a: Closely behind the truck in bad weather because the driver can see farther ahead,b: Farther behind the truck than you would a passenger vehicle to be out of the truck drivers blind spot,c: No more than one car length behind the truck,d: None of the above
note: Large trucks have big blind spots directly behind them. You should follow at a greater distance than you would behind a passenger car so you can see the truck’s mirrors and give yourself more time to react. If you cannot see the truck’s side mirrors, the driver cannot see you.

question: A safety zone is a specially marked area for passengers to get on or off buses or trolleys. You may not drive through a safety zone:
options: a: Only when a bus or trolley is present.,b: Only when a bus or trolley is unloading passengers.,c: At any time or for any reason.
note: Safety zones are reserved areas for pedestrians boarding or leaving buses or streetcars. They are marked on the roadway and are never for vehicle travel. You must not drive through a safety zone at any time, even if no bus or trolley is present.

question: No zones" are areas around trucks where cars:
options: a: Disappear into blind spots or are so close that they restrict the truck driver's ability to stop and maneuver safely.,b: Have sufficient space to travel behind the truck.,c: Have several car lengths between their vehicle and the truck.
note: No Zones are the large blind spots around trucks where your car may be hidden from the truck driver or so close that the driver cannot safely stop or maneuver. Staying out of these areas gives the truck driver room to see you and react safely.

question: Extra space in front of a large truck is needed for:
options: a: Other drivers to merge onto the freeway.,b: The truck driver to stop the vehicle.,c: Other drivers when they want to slow down.
note: Large trucks are heavy and need a much longer distance to stop than passenger cars. Truck drivers leave extra space in front of their vehicles so they have enough room to brake safely if traffic slows or stops suddenly.

question: When sharing the road with a large truck, remember to:
options: a: Follow the large vehicle closely to reduce wind drag on your vehicle.,b: Avoid driving beside it for long stretches of time.,c: Drive on its right side when on curves and hills.
note: You should avoid driving alongside a large truck for long periods because the driver may not see you and has limited room to maneuver. Pass on the left, move ahead, and avoid lingering in the truck’s blind spots.

question: Increase your following distance when driving behind a large vehicle:
options: a: To better see around the sides of the vehicle.,b: Because other drivers tend to pull behind large vehicles before trying to pass them.,c: Because following too closely will get you caught in the vehicle's slipstream.
note: When you follow a large truck too closely, you cannot see the road ahead or react to hazards in time. Leaving extra following distance lets you see around the truck, gives you more time to stop, and reduces the risk of a rear‑end collision.

question: Stopping distances and severity of crashes:
options: a: Decrease as vehicle speed increases.,b: Are not affected by vehicle speed.,c: Increase as vehicle speed increases.
note: Stopping distance increases as speed increases. The faster and heavier a vehicle is, the more time and distance it needs to come to a complete stop. This is why high speeds make crashes more severe and why you must leave more following distance at higher speeds.

question: Which of the following statements about blind spots is true?
options: a: They are eliminated if you have one outside mirror on each side of the vehicle.,b: Large trucks have bigger blind spots than most passenger vehicles.,c: Blind spots can be checked by looking in your rearview mirrors.
note: Large trucks have much larger blind spots, often called No Zones, along the sides, front, and rear of the vehicle. Even with big mirrors, a car can completely disappear in these areas. If you cannot see the truck driver’s mirrors, the driver likely cannot see you.

question: What is true regarding big trucks?
options: a: They take longer to stop than passenger vehicles.,b: They all have air brakes that allow them to stop quickly.,c: They are more maneuverable than passenger vehicles.
note: Big trucks generally need more time and distance to stop than passenger vehicles traveling at the same speed because of their greater weight and momentum. This is why you should never cut closely in front of a truck and should allow extra space when merging or changing lanes near them.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You must always look carefully for motorcycles before you change lanes or make a left turn because they
options: a: Have the right-of-way,b: Are hard to see,c: Are driven too fast
note: Motorcycles are smaller and narrower than cars, so they are much easier to miss in mirrors and blind spots, especially when you are changing lanes or turning left. Always look carefully and check blind spots for motorcycles before moving, because they can be hidden from view even when they are close.

question: When following a motorcycle, drivers must remember that motorcycles can ____________ than other vehicles.
options: a: Accelerate much faster,b: Stop much more quickly,c: Stop much more slowly
note: Motorcycles can usually stop more quickly than most cars because they are lighter and have powerful brakes. When following a motorcycle, leave extra following distance so you have enough time to react if the rider brakes suddenly or loses control.

question: Which statement is true about motorcyclists and motorists?
options: a: Motorcyclists have the same rights/responsibilities as other motorists,b: Motorcyclists are heavier than other vehicles and are less affected by wind/rain,c: Motorcyclists are not allowed to drive faster than other traffic during congested road conditions
note: Motorcyclists are considered drivers of vehicles and must obey the same traffic laws as other motorists. They have the same rights to use the road and the same responsibilities, such as stopping for signals, yielding when required, and following speed limits.

question: You are driving on a city street and see an emergency vehicle with flashing lights behind you. What should you do?
options: a: Drive to the right edge of the road and slow down.,b: Drive to the right edge of the road and stop.,c: Stay in your lane slow down and let it pass.
note: When an emergency vehicle approaches from behind with lights and siren on, you must move to the right edge of the road and stop until it has passed, as long as it is safe to do so. This creates a clear path and prevents sudden conflicts with the emergency vehicle.

question: Children on bicycles should be given extra space by motor vehicle operators because:
options: a: They do not have the same physical reflexes as adults.,b: They are smaller and more difficult to see than adults.,c: Both of the above.
note: Children on bicycles need extra space because they are physically smaller and harder to see, and they usually have less-developed coordination, judgment, and reflexes than adults. They may wobble, swerve, or enter the roadway unexpectedly, so drivers must slow down and give them a wide margin.

question: Motorcycles, scooters, and mopeds are not easy to see; therefore, you should:
options: a: Slow down when driving.,b: Make constant visual checks.,c: Share a lane with a motorcycle.
note: Motorcycles, scooters, and mopeds are small and can easily be hidden in blind spots or behind other vehicles. You should make frequent, deliberate visual checks—especially before changing lanes, turning, or entering traffic—to be sure you see them. Never try to share the same lane side‑by‑side with a motorcycle; they are entitled to a full lane.

question: When driving on gravel or dirt roads:
options: a: Your tires grip the road better than when you are driving on pavement.,b: Your tires do not have as much traction as they do on pavement,c: Visibility is better than on pavement.
note: On gravel or dirt roads, your tires have less traction than on paved roads. Loose surfaces make it easier to skid and harder to stop, so you should slow down and increase your following distance. Because traction is reduced, you must steer, accelerate, and brake more gently than you would on pavement.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You must look for bicyclists in the same lanes used by motor vehicles because they:
options: a: Must ride facing oncoming traffic.,b: Illegally share lanes with motor vehicles.,c: Are entitled to share the road with motor vehicles.
note: Bicyclists are legal road users and generally must ride in the same direction as traffic. They are entitled to use the roadway and often travel in the same lanes as motor vehicles. You must look for them, yield when required, and give them enough space because they have the same basic rights and responsibilities as other drivers.

question: When you see a NEV ROUTE sign, you should watch out for
options: a: A Nevada law enforcement officer,b: Slow-moving vehicles in the roadway,c: Animal-drawn vehicles
note: A NEV ROUTE sign indicates a route used by Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEVs) or Low‑Speed Vehicles (LSVs). These vehicles typically have a maximum speed of about 25 mph, so you should watch for slow‑moving vehicles in the roadway and be prepared to adjust your speed and following distance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: An orange and red triangular sign on a vehicle always means:
options: a: The vehicle has the right-of-way.,b: Slow-moving vehicle.,c: Shoulder work ahead.
note: An orange and red triangular emblem on the rear of a vehicle is the slow‑moving vehicle symbol. It warns that the vehicle usually travels at 25 mph or less, such as farm equipment or some road maintenance vehicles. When you see this sign, slow down and be prepared to pass only when it is safe and legal.

question: Large trucks are likely to lose speed when:
options: a: Driving up long or steep hills.,b: Driving in long tunnels.,c: Driving down long or steep hills.
note: Large, heavy vehicles like trucks slow down when climbing long or steep hills because their engines must work harder against gravity. You should expect them to lose speed on upgrades and be prepared for slower traffic in those areas.

question: You see pedestrians near the road. You should:
options: a: Sound your horn and maintain your speed.,b: Speed up to clear the area quickly.,c: Slow down, be prepared to stop, and pass with caution.
note: When you see pedestrians near the road, you must be prepared to yield and protect them. Slow down, be ready to stop, and pass with caution, giving them plenty of space. Never speed up or use your horn to force pedestrians out of the way.

question: If you are driving and you see animals standing near the roadway:
options: a: Speed up to scare them away.,b: Slow down and proceed with caution.,c: Quickly swerve into the next lane.
note: Animals near or on the roadway can move unpredictably. You should slow down, be prepared to stop, and pass only when you can do so safely. Do not speed up or swerve suddenly, as that can cause you to lose control or collide with other vehicles.

question: When used on roadways, bicycles are considered:
options: a: Hazards.,b: Vehicles.,c: Dangerous.
note: Bicycles are treated as vehicles on the road. Bicyclists generally have the same rights and responsibilities as drivers of cars: they must obey traffic signals and signs, ride in the correct direction, and follow lane rules, and other drivers must yield to them when required by law.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a bicyclist is making a left turn:
options: a: They may use the appropriate left-turn lane or position, like other vehicles, when safe.,b: They may cut across all lanes without regard to traffic.,c: They may wait on the side of the road and complete the turn in two stages when safe.
note: A bicyclist making a left turn may move into the appropriate left-turn lane or left side of the lane, just like a car, when it is safe and after signaling. They may also use a two-stage (box) turn from the right side, but they are never allowed to cut unpredictably across lanes.

question: Bicycle riders must
options: a: Ride facing traffic when there is no bike lane,b: Be given a safe amount of space when being passed by automobile drivers,c: Never walk the bicycle across the street
note: Bicyclists are entitled to space on the road just like other vehicles. When passing a bicyclist, drivers must leave a safe clearance—commonly at least three feet where specified by law—and should not attempt to pass if they cannot provide that space. Bicyclists should ride in the same direction as traffic, and they may walk their bicycle across the street when needed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You want to pass a bicyclist riding on the right edge of your lane. You
options: a: Must not squeeze past the bicyclist,b: May not pass the bicyclist for any reason,c: Must honk your horn before passing the bicyclist
note: You must never try to squeeze past a bicyclist in the same narrow lane. When passing, move over and leave at least three feet of space where required by law. If you cannot safely give that space because of traffic or road conditions, wait behind the bicyclist until it is safe to pass. Honking is not a substitute for safe clearance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are driving behind a motorcycle and want to pass. You must:
options: a: Stay in your lane and pass only if you can safely share the lane with the motorcycle.,b: Blow your horn to make the motorcycle move onto the shoulder so that you can pass.,c: Move completely into the left lane and keep your vehicle entirely in that lane while passing the motorcycle.
note: Motorcycles are entitled to the full use of a lane, just like any other motor vehicle. When you pass a motorcycle, you must change lanes completely so your vehicle is fully in the passing lane before, during, and after the pass. Do not share or straddle the motorcycle’s lane, and never force the rider onto the shoulder.

question: You want to pass a bicyclist in a narrow traffic lane when an oncoming vehicle is approaching. You should:
options: a: Honk your horn then pass the bicyclist.,b: Slow down and let the vehicle pass you before you pass the bicyclist.,c: Wait until the bicyclist rides off the roadway.
note: On a narrow lane with oncoming traffic, you must not try to squeeze between the bicyclist and the oncoming vehicle. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass first.
