Then, when there is no oncoming traffic and you can provide at least three feet of clearance (or more if needed), pass the bicyclist safely. Do not rely on your horn to create space.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If traffic light is red, but a police officer or fire fighter on duty tells you to go ahead, you should
options: a: Wait for the green light,b: Do as he or she tells you,c: Report him or her to police
note: When a law enforcement officer or firefighter on duty directs you, you must follow their instructions even if they conflict with traffic signals or signs. Their directions temporarily override normal traffic controls to keep traffic and people safe.

question: Which sign on a truck means that the truck's load is potentially dangerous?
options: a: Octagonal.,b: Diamond shaped.,c: Rectangular wide.,d: None of the above
note: Diamond-shaped placards on trucks indicate hazardous materials. These signs warn that the load may be dangerous, such as flammable, explosive, toxic, or corrosive substances, so other drivers and emergency responders can take proper precautions.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Drivers are required to obey instructions from:
options: a: Security guards patrolling parking lots.,b: Other drivers whose vehicles are broken down on the roadway.,c: Flaggers (signal persons) at construction sites.
note: Drivers must obey flaggers (signal persons) at construction or work zones because they are authorized to control traffic for safety. Instructions from other drivers or private security guards in parking lots are not legally binding traffic control in the same way.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Fines in a construction zone are:
options: a: Doubled.,b: Tripled.,c: Cut in half.
note: In many states, fines are increased—often doubled—in highway construction or maintenance zones when workers are present. Higher fines encourage drivers to slow down and pay extra attention to protect road workers and other drivers.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If a traffic signal light is green and a police officer signals for you to stop, you should:
options: a: Obey the officer.,b: Obey the traffic signal.,c: Do what the vehicle in front of you does.
note: A police officer’s directions always override traffic signals and signs. If the light is green but an officer signals you to stop, you must stop, because the officer is managing traffic for safety or an emergency situation.

question: If you are continually being passed on the right and the left while driving in the center lane of an expressway, you should:
options: a: Stay in the center lane.,b: Move to the lane on your right.,c: Move to the lane on your left.
note: On multilane highways, slower traffic should keep right. If you are in the center lane and vehicles are passing you on both sides, you are going slower than the flow of traffic. To avoid blocking traffic and to drive more safely, move to the right lane so faster vehicles can pass on your left.

question: There is a vehicle stopped on the right shoulder of the road with its hazard lights on. You should:
options: a: Change lanes to the left if safe and adjust your speed.,b: Slow down and pass very carefully.,c: Stop your vehicle until you can see what has happened.
note: When you see a vehicle stopped on the shoulder with hazard lights on, you should slow down and pass with extra caution, and change lanes away from it if you can do so safely. This reduces the risk of hitting a person who may be outside the vehicle or a door that might open unexpectedly. You do not need to stop unless there is an obvious emergency requiring your help or directions from law enforcement.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When driving in a construction zone:
options: a: Slightly increase your speed.,b: Expect the unexpected.,c: Expect construction workers to yield to motorists.
note: Construction zones often have workers close to traffic, lane shifts, uneven pavement, and slow-moving equipment. Because conditions can change quickly, you must stay alert, obey all signs and flaggers, and be ready for anything unexpected, such as sudden stops or workers entering the lane.

question: When driving in work zones, you should:
options: a: Increase your speed to get through the zone as quickly as possible.,b: Reduce your speed and be prepared to stop suddenly.,c: Maintain your normal speed the whole way through the zone.
note: In work zones you should slow down, leave extra following distance, and be prepared to stop suddenly. Lanes may narrow, traffic may stop without warning, and workers or equipment may enter the roadway. Driving at a reduced, cautious speed gives you more time to react safely.

question: Which of the following is a dangerous habit when driving in work zones?
options: a: Tailgating another vehicle,b: Failing to carefully watch for workers and moving equipment,c: Both of the above
note: In work zones, following too closely (tailgating) is dangerous because traffic can slow or stop suddenly. Failing to watch carefully for workers and moving equipment is also hazardous, since workers may be close to traffic and equipment may enter your lane. Both behaviors greatly increase the risk of a crash, so you must avoid them.

question: Which of the following is true about vehicles displaying a diamond-shaped sign that indicates a hazardous load?
options: a: They are not allowed to drive on freeways.,b: They must stop before crossing railroad tracks.,c: They are not allowed to exceed 35 mph.
note: A diamond-shaped placard on a vehicle indicates it is carrying hazardous materials. Federal and state rules require many placarded hazardous‑materials vehicles to stop before crossing railroad tracks so the driver can check for trains. This is a safety measure because hazardous cargo can cause severe damage if a collision occurs on the tracks.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which of these statements is true about roadwork zones?
options: a: Fines are the same for violations committed in work zones as they are under normal traffic conditions.,b: You must ‘Slow for the Cone Zone’,c: Slow down only if you think workers are present.
note: In roadwork zones, you must reduce your speed and drive with extra caution. The phrase “Slow for the Cone Zone” reminds drivers to slow down, watch for workers and equipment, and be prepared for sudden stops or lane changes. Fines are often higher in work zones, and you must slow even if you do not immediately see workers present.

question: Work zone barriers, drums, cones, and signs are used to:
options: a: Make drivers angry about slow traffic.,b: Inconvenience drivers.,c: Keep traffic out of hazardous work zones.
note: Work zone barriers, drums, cones, and signs are placed to separate traffic from construction areas and guide drivers safely through or around the work zone. They keep vehicles out of hazardous areas where workers, equipment, uneven pavement, or open trenches may be present.

question: You see a signal person at a road construction site ahead. You should obey his or her instructions:
options: a: Only if you see orange cones on the road ahead.,b: Unless they conflict with existing signs,c: At all times.
note: Flaggers and other signal persons in construction zones have legal authority to direct traffic. You must obey their instructions at all times, even if they differ from posted signs or signals, because they are managing real‑time hazards and lane changes in the work area.

question: What should you do when there is a school bus ahead that starts flashing yellow warning lights?
options: a: Slow down and prepare to stop.,b: Stop immediately and remain stopped.,c: Cautiously pass the school bus on the left.
note: Flashing yellow lights on a school bus mean the bus is preparing to stop to load or unload children. You must slow down, be ready to stop, and watch for children near the roadway. You are required to stop when the red lights begin flashing and the stop arm is extended; do not pass the bus once it is preparing to stop.

question: When is it required for you to obey directions from a crossing guard?
options: a: At all times.,b: During school hours only.,c: Only when children are present in front of a school.
note: You must obey a crossing guard’s directions whenever they are giving traffic control instructions, not just during school hours or only when children are visible. Crossing guards have legal authority similar to traffic control devices, so their directions must be followed at all times they are on duty.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Driving slowly in front of traffic in the far left (last) lane on any freeway
options: a: Can result in a traffic citation for impeding traffic in the left lane in many states.,b: Is recommended because it forces others to slow down.,c: Can frustrate other drivers, increase unsafe lane changes, and may lead to a citation for impeding traffic.
note: The far left lane on a freeway is generally intended for faster traffic and passing. Driving much slower than the flow in that lane can cause other drivers to brake or weave, increasing the risk of crashes and road rage. Even if your exact speed is at or below the limit, you should move right if you are impeding faster traffic to keep traffic flowing smoothly and safely.

question: Should you always drive slower than other traffic?
options: a: No you can block traffic when you drive too slowly.,b: Yes it is a good defensive driving technique.,c: Yes it is always safer than driving faster.
note: You should drive at a speed that matches safe traffic flow and road conditions, not simply slower than everyone else. Driving much slower than surrounding traffic when it is not necessary can cause other drivers to brake or change lanes abruptly and can be illegal if you unnecessarily block normal traffic flow.

question: If you drive more slowly than the flow of traffic, you will most likely:
options: a: Interfere with traffic and receive a ticket.,b: Improve traffic flow.,c: Demonstrate defensive driving techniques.
note: Driving much slower than the normal flow of traffic can be just as dangerous as speeding because it causes other drivers to brake, change lanes, or make sudden moves. If you unnecessarily block or interfere with normal and reasonable traffic flow, you can be cited. Always drive at a safe speed for conditions while also keeping with the general flow, without exceeding the speed limit.

question: In traffic moving at 50 to 55 mph, you are least likely to have an accident if you:
options: a: Drive a few miles per hour faster than most other vehicles.,b: Stay within that speed range.,c: Drive a few miles per hour slower than most other vehicles.
note: You are safest when you travel at a speed that matches the general flow of traffic, as long as it is within the posted speed limit and safe for conditions. Driving a little faster or a little slower than surrounding traffic forces more lane changes and passing, which increases the chance of collisions. In 50–55 mph traffic, staying within that range and with the flow is usually the safest choice.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Vehicles stopped behind a school bus with its red lights flashing must remain stopped until:
options: a: All students are off the bus.,b: The stop arm is retracted.,c: The stop arm is retracted and the bus resumes motion.
note: When a school bus has its red lights flashing and stop arm extended, you must stop and remain stopped until the red lights stop flashing and the stop arm is retracted. The bus does not have to start moving before you proceed; once the signals are off and the arm is in, it is your indication that children are no longer crossing and it is safe to go, if the road is clear.

question: When a school bus is picking up or dropping off children, you must:
options: a: Stop.,b: Stop if you are driving in the same direction.,c: Slow down and be prepared to stop.
note: When a school bus is picking up or dropping off children and its red lights are flashing, you must stop, whether you are approaching from behind or from the opposite direction (except in specific divided-highway exceptions defined by state law). Stopping in both directions protects children who may cross the road in front of the bus.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When a school bus is stopped ahead on your side of the road with its red lights flashing, you must:
options: a: Slow to a speed no faster than 10 mph.,b: Stop until the lights stop flashing.,c: Change lanes and pass cautiously.
note: If a school bus ahead of you on your side of the road has its red lights flashing, you must come to a complete stop and remain stopped until the red lights stop flashing. The flashing red lights and stop arm mean children may be crossing the road, so you cannot pass the bus until those signals are turned off.

question: Which of these vehicles must always stop before crossing railroad tracks?
options: a: Tank trucks marked with hazardous materials placards.,b: Motor homes or pickup trucks towing a boat trailer.,c: Any vehicle with three or more axles and weighing more than 4,000 pounds.
note: Vehicles carrying certain hazardous materials, such as tank trucks with hazardous materials placards, must always stop before crossing railroad tracks so the driver can look and listen for trains and be sure the tracks are clear. This extra precaution reduces the risk of a catastrophic crash or spill if a train is approaching.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do when traffic is slow and heavy, and you must cross railroad tracks before reaching the upcoming intersection?
options: a: Begin crossing when the vehicle in front of you is crossing the tracks.,b: Wait on the tracks until the stoplight at the intersection turns green.,c: Wait until you can completely cross the tracks before proceeding.
note: You must never stop on railroad tracks. In slow or heavy traffic, wait until there is enough space on the far side of the tracks for your entire vehicle before you start across. If you enter the crossing without enough room, you could be trapped on the tracks if traffic stops, putting you at serious risk if a train approaches.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You must stop at the intersection ahead. Just before the intersection, you have to cross railroad tracks. You should stop before you cross the railroad tracks when
options: a: You don’t have room to completely cross the tracks,b: The crossing is located in a city or town with frequent train traffic,c: You transport two or more children in a passenger vehicle
note: You must never stop on railroad tracks. If there is an intersection just beyond the tracks, do not move forward until you are sure there is enough space for your entire vehicle to clear the tracks. If you do not have room to completely cross, stop and wait before the tracks until traffic ahead moves.

question: Always stop before crossing railroad tracks when:
options: a: There isn't room on the other side for you to completely cross the tracks.,b: The railroad crossing is located in a city or town that has frequent train traffic.,c: You are transporting two or more young children in a passenger vehicle.
note: According to page 51, 'Never stop on the railroad tracks. Wait and do not begin proceeding if you do not have enough room to completely cross the tracks. If you are on the tracks, you risk injury or death.'

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you come to an intersection and your view to the side is blocked, you should:
options: a: Slow down and look both ways.,b: Maintain your speed and look both ways.,c: Stop.
note: At an intersection where your view is blocked, you must first stop at the limit line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection. After stopping, move forward slowly until you can see clearly and check for traffic in all directions. Simply slowing without stopping is not enough when your view is obstructed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When crossing a sidewalk to enter traffic from an alley or driveway, drivers should:
options: a: Stop only if pedestrians are on the sidewalk.,b: Stop before driving onto the sidewalk or sidewalk area.,c: Expect pedestrians on the sidewalk to yield the right-of-way.
note: When exiting an alley or driveway across a sidewalk, you must stop before driving onto the sidewalk area. Look carefully for pedestrians and bicyclists and yield to them. Only proceed when the sidewalk is clear and it is safe to enter the roadway.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When may you legally drive around or under a railroad crossing gate?
options: a: Never.,b: When you can see clearly in both directions.,c: When the warning lights are not flashing.
note: It is illegal and extremely dangerous to drive around or under a railroad crossing gate at any time. You must wait until the gates are fully raised and the warning lights and bells have stopped before crossing the tracks.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which statement is true?
options: a: You should put on your cruise control near a railroad crossing to maintain a constant speed.,b: You must stop at a railroad crossing when directed to do so by a flagger or stop sign.,c: You have the right-of-way at a railroad crossing and do not need to stop.
note: At railroad crossings, you must obey all traffic control devices and any flagger directing traffic. If a stop sign, signal, or flagger indicates you must stop, do so at least 15 feet from the nearest rail and proceed only when it is clearly safe. Trains always have the right-of-way at crossings.

question: You have stopped for a train at a railroad crossing. After the train passes, you should:
options: a: Wait for signal lights to stop flashing.,b: Look for a second train.,c: Both of the above.
note: After a train passes, you must not proceed until the warning devices stop operating and you have checked for another train. Wait until the red lights stop flashing and any gates are fully raised, then look carefully in both directions for a second train before crossing. Trains can come from either direction, and a second train may be hidden by the first.

question: A passenger vehicle may NOT tow
options: a: One trailer,b: Another passenger vehicle,c: Two trailers
note: A passenger vehicle may tow one trailer, and in some states under specific conditions, two trailers, but it may not tow another passenger vehicle on the highway in normal driving. Towing another passenger vehicle generally requires special equipment and is restricted to tow trucks or emergency situations, not ordinary passenger vehicles.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A person may legally ride in the back of a pickup truck when:
options: a: The sides of the pickup bed are at least 24 inches high.,b: The back of the pickup is covered with a camper shell.,c: In a secured seat and while using an approved safety belt.
note: People may ride in the back of a pickup only if they are in properly installed, secure seats and are using approved safety belts. Riding loose in the cargo area, even with high sides or a camper shell, is unsafe and not allowed because occupants can be thrown out or severely injured in a sudden stop or crash.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Abandoning an animal on the highway may result in:
options: a: Jail time.,b: A point against your license.,c: No legal consequences.
note: Abandoning or dumping an animal on a highway is a crime. It can result in a fine, jail time, or both, because it endangers the animal, other drivers, and violates animal cruelty and littering laws.

question: Animals may be transported in the back of a pickup truck only if:
options: a: The sides of the truck bed are at least 18 inches high.,b: They are properly secured.,c: The tailgate of the truck is closed.
note: Animals may only be transported in the back of a pickup or other truck if they are properly secured so they cannot fall, jump, or be thrown from the vehicle. Proper securing protects the animal and prevents sudden road hazards for other drivers.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you are repeatedly convicted for traffic violations
options: a: DMV may impound your vehicle,b: Your driving privilege may be suspended by DMV,c: Both of the above
note: DMV does monitor your driving record and can suspend or revoke your driving privilege if you accumulate too many points or fail to appear in court. However, repeated traffic violations normally result in action against your license, not impoundment of your vehicle. Vehicle impound is usually tied to specific offenses (such as DUI, driving on a suspended license, or certain criminal violations), not simply having multiple traffic convictions.

question: Which of the following is an example of a safe driving practice?
options: a: Staring only at the middle of the road.,b: Always keep your eyes moving to scan the surroundings.,c: Using your high-beam headlights in the fog
note: Safe drivers constantly scan the road and their surroundings instead of staring at one fixed point. By keeping your eyes moving and looking at least 10–15 seconds ahead, you can spot hazards early and have more time to react. Using high beams in fog is unsafe because the light reflects back and reduces visibility.

question: Which of the following should you do if you are being followed by a tailgater?
options: a: Change lanes and allow the tailgater to pass.,b: Tap the brakes to signal you are moving at a slower pace.,c: Increase your speed to match the speed of the vehicle.
note: When someone is following too closely, the safest response is to create space and let them pass when it is safe. Change lanes or move to the right when possible and allow the tailgater to go by. Do not speed up to match their speed, and do not tap your brakes to “send a message,” as this can increase the risk of a rear-end collision.

question: If you become angry or upset, you should
options: a: Go for a drive to forget your problems,b: 'Cool off' before driving,c: Control your emotions while driving
note: If you are angry or very upset, you should not drive until you have calmed down. Strong emotions can make you react aggressively, take risks, or miss hazards. The safest choice is to cool off first, then drive only when you can stay calm and focused.

question: The three-second rule applies to the space ______ of your vehicle.
options: a: To the sides,b: Ahead,c: In the back
note: The 'three-second rule' is a driving rule that helps you estimate how closely you should follow other vehicles. 'When the vehicle in front of you passes a certain point, such as a sign, count three seconds. If you pass the same point before you finish counting, you are following too closely.'

question: A driver cuts off another vehicle, or threatens another motorist or a pedestrian. These are examples of
options: a: Excessive driving,b: Defensive driving,c: Road rage
note: Road rage is aggressive or angry driving behavior, such as cutting off other vehicles, yelling, making threats, or using your vehicle to intimidate others. These actions are dangerous, can lead to crashes, and may be crimes. Safe drivers avoid escalating conflicts and stay calm around aggressive drivers.

question: Tailgating
options: a: Is a defensive driving technique,b: Cannot result in a traffic citation,c: Can frustrate other drivers and make them angry
note: Tailgating means following another vehicle too closely. It reduces your time to react if the vehicle ahead slows or stops and often makes other drivers nervous or angry, increasing the risk of crashes and road rage. Always leave a safe following distance so you can stop smoothly if needed.

question: While driving, you should look 10 to 15 seconds ahead of you
options: a: Because it’s a legal requirement,b: And focus on the middle of the road,c: To see potential hazards early
note: Looking 10–15 seconds ahead lets you spot hazards early, giving you time to slow, change lanes, or stop smoothly instead of making sudden last‑second moves. This is a core safe‑driving habit, not just a legal formality.

question: When a hazard is seen ahead, reaction distance
options: a: Equals total stopping distance minus perception distance,b: Is how far a vehicle will continue to travel in ideal conditions before the driver hits the brakes,c: Is the sum of perception distance and braking distance
note: Reaction distance is how far your vehicle travels from the moment you see a hazard until you actually start to brake. During this time you are reacting, but the brakes have not yet begun to slow the car. It is not the same as braking distance, and it is not the sum of perception and braking distances.

question: Looking down the road to where your vehicle will be in about 10 seconds helps you to
options: a: enjoy the scenery,b: avoid last minute moves,c: see hazards inside your car
note: By looking ahead to where your vehicle will be in about 10 seconds, you can see problems—like slowing traffic, lane closures, or obstacles—early. This advance warning helps you change speed or lanes smoothly instead of making sudden, last‑minute maneuvers.

question: To avoid last minute moves, you should be looking down the road to where your vehicle will be in about
options: a: 5 to 10 seconds,b: 10 to 15 seconds,c: 15 to 20 seconds
note: To avoid last‑minute moves, you should scan well ahead—about 10 to 15 seconds down the road. This longer look‑ahead distance gives you time to notice hazards, adjust your speed, and position your vehicle safely before you reach trouble.

question: Which of the following is a good practice when driving in adverse weather conditions?
options: a: Use cruise control to maintain a consistent speed,b: Increase your following distance,c: Drive at the posted speed limit,d: None of the above
note: In rain, snow, fog, or other adverse conditions, it takes longer to see hazards and to stop. Increasing your following distance gives you extra space and time to brake gently and avoid skids or rear‑end collisions. Cruise control and driving at the posted limit can both be unsafe when traction or visibility is reduced.

question: You are driving in the far right lane of a multi-lane street. A vehicle in the lane to your left moves into your lane causing you to slow down. You should:
options: a: Use your horn to let the driver know they are in your lane.,b: Brake hard and use your emergency flashers.,c: Be prepared to adjust your speed and position to avoid a collision.
note: When another vehicle moves into your lane too closely, your priority is to avoid a collision, not to punish or startle the other driver. Ease off the accelerator and be ready to adjust your speed and lane position to re‑establish a safe following distance. Sudden hard braking or using the horn aggressively can increase the risk of a crash.

question: A driver should:
options: a: Stare directly in front of their car.,b: Only focus on the middle of the road.,c: Watch beside and around their vehicle, checking ahead, mirrors, and side areas regularly.
note: Safe driving requires scanning all around your vehicle, not just straight ahead. You should regularly check the road ahead, your mirrors, and the areas to the sides so you can spot hazards like pedestrians, cyclists, or cars entering from side streets. Keeping track of what is beside and around you gives you time to react safely.

question: A vehicle suddenly cuts in front of you, creating a hazard. What should you do first?
options: a: Honk and step on the brake firmly.,b: Take your foot off the gas pedal.,c: Swerve into the lane next to you.
note: If a vehicle suddenly cuts in front of you, the safest first action is to ease off the accelerator. This helps you quickly increase the space in front of your vehicle without making a sudden, hard move. Once you have reduced speed, you can brake smoothly if needed. Swerving or slamming on the brakes can cause you to lose control or be hit from behind.

question: Allow extra space in front of your vehicle when following a:
options: a: Station wagon.,b: Passenger vehicle.,c: Motorcycle.
note: Motorcycles can stop and maneuver more quickly than larger vehicles, and they are more vulnerable in a collision. You should leave extra following distance when driving behind a motorcycle so you have more time to react if the rider slows or swerves, especially on slippery or uneven surfaces like metal bridge gratings or gravel.

question: As your speed increases, it is important to:
options: a: Turn on your headlights.,b: Look well ahead of your vehicle.,c: Change lanes frequently.
note: As speed increases, you cover more distance in less time, so you must look farther ahead to spot hazards early. Scanning well ahead (about 10–15 seconds down the road) gives you time to see problems, adjust speed, or change lanes smoothly instead of making sudden, unsafe maneuvers.

question: If you are being followed too closely on a two-lane road:
options: a: Gradually reduce your speed and, when safe, allow the tailgater to pass.,b: Speed up to increase the distance between you and the other car.,c: Apply your brakes hard to warn the tailgater.
note: When someone is following too closely on a two‑lane road, you should not brake suddenly or speed up. Instead, maintain control and gradually reduce your speed to increase following distance ahead and make it easier and safer for the tailgater to pass when there is a legal passing opportunity. Sudden braking can cause a rear‑end collision, and speeding up only increases danger.

question: If you encounter an aggressive driver, you should:
options: a: Challenge them.,b: Get out of their way.,c: Speed up.
note: If you encounter an aggressive driver, do not engage, challenge, or try to “win.” The safest response is to stay calm, avoid eye contact, and safely get out of their way by allowing them to pass or creating space. This reduces the chance of a crash or an escalation into road rage.

question: Interstate driving requires drivers to:
options: a: Have the ability to safely drive at increased speeds.,b: Be constantly alert.,c: Both of the above.
note: Interstate driving involves higher speeds and more traffic, so you must be able to safely handle increased speeds and stay constantly alert. You need to manage your speed, maintain safe following distances, and continuously scan mirrors and the road ahead to detect hazards early.

question: To prevent tailgating, drivers should follow the:
options: a: One-second rule.,b: Two-second rule.,c: Three-second rule.
note: Using the three‑second rule helps you maintain a safe following distance. Pick a fixed object ahead; when the vehicle in front passes it, you should be able to count at least “one‑thousand‑one, one‑thousand‑two, one‑thousand‑three” before you reach the same point. This gives you time to react and reduces the chance of rear‑end collisions.

question: To prevent yourself from becoming an aggressive driver:
options: a: Relax and concentrate on driving.,b: Drive above the posted speed limit.,c: Tailgate the driver in front of you.
note: Staying relaxed and concentrating on driving helps prevent aggressive behavior. When you focus on the road, keep a calm attitude, and avoid taking other drivers’ mistakes personally, you are less likely to speed, tailgate, or make risky maneuvers that can lead to crashes or confrontations.

question: What is the benefit of a space cushion around your vehicle?
options: a: Other drivers can cut in front of you,b: If another driver makes a mistake,c: It inflates to protect you from injury in the case of a collision.
note: A space cushion is the open area around your vehicle that gives you room to maneuver. If another driver makes a mistake—such as stopping suddenly, drifting into your lane, or pulling out in front of you—the extra space gives you time and distance to brake, steer, or otherwise avoid a collision.

question: When being followed by a tailgater, which of the following will help you avoid being hit from behind?
options: a: Merging into another lane,b: Decreasing your following distance,c: Changing lanes frequently
note: When someone is tailgating you, the safest response is to create space by letting them pass. Maintain a steady speed, avoid sudden braking, and when it is safe, merge into another lane or move right so the tailgater can go around you. This reduces the risk of being hit from behind.

question: When driving on the highway, consistently looking far ahead of your vehicle:
options: a: Helps you keep up with traffic.,b: Reduces the need for last-minute braking or turning.,c: Allows you to spot upcoming police officers.
note: Looking well ahead on the highway lets you see hazards, slow traffic, and lane changes early so you can adjust smoothly instead of braking or turning at the last second. This improves safety and gives you more time and space to react.

question: When you tailgate other drivers (drive closely to their rear bumper):
options: a: You can frustrate the other drivers and make them angry.,b: Your actions cannot result in a traffic citation.,c: You help reduce traffic congestion.
note: Following too closely can anger or intimidate other drivers and may trigger road rage. It also cuts your view of the road ahead and leaves you too little time to react if the vehicle in front stops suddenly, greatly increasing your crash risk.

question: Which of the following describes the thinking of defensive drivers?
options: a: They know other drivers will do the right thing.,b: They consider what other drivers might do and are prepared to react.,c: They expect no breaks and give none.
note: Defensive drivers constantly scan the road and think about what other drivers might do, such as sudden stops or lane changes. By anticipating others’ actions, they leave extra space and are ready to react safely to unexpected situations.

question: You can help keep the driver behind you a safe distance away from your vehicle by:
options: a: Driving 10 mph faster than the car behind you.,b: Driving 10 mph slower than the car behind you.,c: Maintaining a steady speed.
note: Maintaining a steady speed and not frequently speeding up or slowing down makes it easier for the driver behind you to judge distance and stay back safely. Smooth, predictable driving helps create and maintain safe following space in traffic.

question: You drive defensively when you:
options: a: Put one car length between you and the car ahead.,b: Look only at the car in front of you while driving.,c: Keep your eyes moving to look for possible hazards.
note: Defensive driving means constantly scanning the road, checking mirrors, and watching for potential hazards from all directions. Keeping your eyes moving helps you spot problems early and gives you more time to react safely.

question: You should allow an extra cushion of space:
options: a: When following a station wagon.,b: When following a driver who cannot see the rear of their vehicle.,c: When following a small passenger car.
note: You should leave extra following distance behind large or hard‑to‑see vehicles, such as trucks, buses, or vehicles with blocked rear windows, because their drivers may not see you well and you cannot see around them as easily. More space gives you extra time to react if they stop or turn suddenly.

question: You should increase the distance between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead when you:
options: a: Are following a small passenger vehicle.,b: Are being tailgated by another driver.,c: Are driving more slowly than the posted speed limit.
note: When someone is tailgating you, increase the space in front of your vehicle. A larger gap ahead gives you more room to slow or stop smoothly, reducing the chance that the tailgater will hit you from behind if traffic ahead suddenly changes.

question: To help avoid being hit from the rear by another driver when preparing to turn, you should
options: a: Keep parking lights on at all times,b: Signal at least 100 feet before you turn,c: Check your rearview mirror often
note: To help avoid being hit from the rear when turning, signal well in advance—at least 100 feet before you turn in most areas (and more at higher speeds). Early, clear signaling gives drivers behind you time to slow down and adjust, which greatly reduces the risk of a rear‑end collision.

question: You may open your vehicle's door on the traffic side
options: a: At any time while parked,b: To leave but not to enter your vehicle,c: Only when it is safe
note: You may only open your door on the traffic side when it is safe and will not interfere with traffic or cyclists. Always check mirrors and blind spots first, and do not leave the door open longer than necessary.

question: You see a vehicle approaching from the rear. When you check your mirror again to change lanes, you no longer see the vehicle. You should
options: a: Turn your signal on and change lanes slowly,b: Look over your shoulder to be sure the vehicle isn’t in your blind spot,c: Check your outside mirror to see if the vehicle is in your blind spot
note: Before changing lanes, always check your mirrors and then look over your shoulder to check your blind spot. A vehicle that disappears from your mirror may be alongside you where mirrors cannot see, so a quick glance over the appropriate shoulder is necessary before moving into the next lane.

question: Blind spots are:
options: a: Spots in your vision when you become fatigued.,b: Areas of the road that cannot be seen in a vehicle's mirrors.,c: Traffic control devices.
note: Blind spots are the areas around your vehicle that you cannot see with your mirrors alone. Even with properly adjusted mirrors, there will be zones to the side and slightly behind your vehicle that require a head check over your shoulder to see other traffic.

question: Check your rearview mirrors:
options: a: Often to see how traffic is moving behind you.,b: To see if a vehicle is in your blind spot.,c: Only when you are slowing down.
note: You should check your rearview mirror often to stay aware of traffic behind you. Knowing what is happening to the rear helps you react early to fast-approaching vehicles, prepare for lane changes, and reduce the risk of rear-end collisions.

question: To know where traffic is behind you:
options: a: Frequently check your rearview mirror.,b: Turn and look out your back window.,c: Keep other vehicles out of your blind spots.
note: To stay aware of traffic behind you, check your rearview mirror frequently. Regular mirror checks help you notice vehicles that are following too closely, approaching quickly, or preparing to pass, so you can adjust your driving safely.

question: To see vehicles in your blind spots, you should check:
options: a: The inside rearview mirror.,b: The outside rearview mirror.,c: Over your shoulders.
note: Blind spots are areas you cannot see with your mirrors alone. To check them, you must briefly turn your head and look over your right or left shoulder before changing lanes or merging. Inside and outside mirrors are important, but they do not fully show vehicles in your blind spots.

question: When changing lanes, you can check your blind spot by:
options: a: Using the inside rearview mirror.,b: Turning your head and looking over your shoulder.,c: Using your side mirror.
note: Before changing lanes, always check your mirrors and then turn your head to look over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move. This quick shoulder check lets you see into your blind spot, where a vehicle may be hidden from your mirrors.

question: When driving on an interstate, to avoid traffic merging from on-ramps to your right, the best thing to do is to:
options: a: Change lanes to the left.,b: Slow down.,c: Maintain your speed and position.
note: On freeways, you should help traffic merge safely. If vehicles are entering from an on‑ramp to your right, the safest choice is usually to change one lane to the left if it is clear and legal. This creates space for merging traffic and reduces sudden braking or lane changes.

question: When passing a row of parked vehicles, you should:
options: a: Be prepared for a person or vehicle to unexpectedly enter your lane.,b: Expect all other drivers and pedestrians to respect your right-of-way.,c: Drive closely to the parked vehicles to allow more room for moving traffic.
note: When passing parked vehicles, leave extra space and be ready for doors to open, people to step out, or cars to pull away from the curb. Never assume others will yield to you; instead, slow down and position your vehicle to give yourself room to react.

question: You are on the freeway and traffic is merging into your lane. You should:
options: a: Make room for the merging traffic,b: Assert your right-of-way by driving faster.,c: Always maintain your position.
note: Freeway traffic generally has the right-of-way over vehicles entering from an on‑ramp, but safe driving requires cooperation. When you see vehicles merging into your lane, you should, when possible, adjust your speed or change lanes to create a safe gap. Making room reduces the risk of sudden braking or side‑swipes and helps traffic flow smoothly.

question: What is the main reason night driving is more difficult than daytime driving?
options: a: The use of headlight is required by law,b: Driving within the range of your headlights is required,c: Reduced visibility
note: Night driving is harder mainly because you cannot see as far or as clearly as in daylight. Headlights limit how much of the road and surroundings you can see, making it harder to detect hazards, judge distances, and see pedestrians or animals. Because visibility is reduced, you must slow down and ensure you can stop within the distance you can see ahead.

question: When driving at night with no other vehicles ahead, a driver should use
options: a: High beam lights,b: Low-beam lights,c: Parking lights
note: When there are no vehicles ahead of you and no oncoming traffic, you should use your high‑beam headlights. High beams let you see farther down the road and to the sides, giving you more time to react to hazards. Dim your high beams to low beams when you are following another vehicle closely or when an oncoming vehicle is within the legal dimming distance (commonly about 500 feet).

question: It is more dangerous to drive at night than during the day because:
options: a: You cannot see as far ahead at night.,b: The road is always more slippery at night.,c: Your reaction time is slower at night.
note: Driving at night is more dangerous primarily because you cannot see as far ahead as you can during the day. Limited visibility reduces the time you have to detect and react to hazards, curves, and stopped vehicles. Even with headlights, your view is restricted, so you must adjust your speed to ensure you can stop within the distance you can see.

question: Night driving presents unique problems because:
options: a: The speed limit is increased at night.,b: There are fewer cars on the roads at night.,c: Distance and vehicle speed are difficult to judge in the dark.
note: At night, depth perception and peripheral vision are reduced, and headlights can create glare and shadows. This makes it harder to judge how far away other vehicles are and how fast they are moving. Because distance and speed are more difficult to judge in the dark, you should increase your following distance and drive at a speed that allows you to react safely.

question: To avoid glare from the headlights of an approaching car:
options: a: Look briefly toward the right side of the road.,b: Stay focused on the centerline on the road.,c: Flash your high beams.
note: Looking briefly toward the right edge of your lane reduces the glare from oncoming headlights and helps you keep your lane position using the right edge line or curb as a guide. You should not stare at the oncoming lights or respond by using your own high beams, because that can temporarily blind both you and the other driver.

question: When driving at night on a dimly lit street, you should:
options: a: Drive slowly enough that you can stop within the area illuminated by your headlights.,b: Turn on your high beam headlights to better see the vehicles ahead of you.,c: Keep the instrument panel lights bright to be more visible to other drivers.
note: At night you must always be able to stop within the distance you can see with your headlights. If you drive faster than that, you may not have enough time to react to hazards that appear in the dark. Use low beams in dimly lit areas when other traffic is present, and adjust your speed so you can safely stop within the illuminated area.

question: While driving at night, a vehicle coming toward you has its high beams on, making it hard for you to see the road ahead. You should:
options: a: Look ahead toward the left edge of your lane.,b: Look ahead toward the right edge of your lane.,c: Look straight ahead in your lane.
note: When an oncoming driver leaves high beams on, looking toward the right edge of your lane helps you avoid being blinded while still keeping your vehicle correctly positioned. Use the right edge line or curb as a reference until the vehicle passes, rather than staring into the bright lights or straight ahead where the glare is strongest.

question: What should drivers do in case of a brake failure?
options: a: Sound your horn and tie a white cloth or other visible marker only after you have safely stopped off the roadway.,b: Brake lightly and continue driving at the same speed.,c: Shift to a lower gear and use the engine and parking brake to help slow and stop the vehicle.
note: If your brakes fail, take your foot off the accelerator and shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the vehicle. Then, if possible, pump the brake pedal to try to build up pressure, and use the parking brake gradually to avoid locking the wheels. Steer to a safe area and use your horn and lights to warn others. Tying a cloth to the car or braking lightly alone will not safely stop a vehicle with failed brakes.

question: ABS is the acronym for
options: a: Anti-lock Brake System,b: Anti-Braking System,c: Asphalt-Braking System
note: ABS stands for Anti-lock Brake System. This system prevents the wheels from locking up during hard braking, helping you maintain steering control. With ABS, you generally apply firm, continuous pressure to the brake pedal rather than pumping the brakes.

question: Continuous hard braking on ice and snow often:
options: a: Helps you stop faster.,b: Locks the front wheels of a vehicle,c: Keeps the brakes from freezing.
note: On ice and snow, pressing the brake pedal hard can cause the wheels to lock and slide instead of rolling. Locked front wheels reduce your ability to steer and control the vehicle. To stop safely on slippery roads, brake gently and progressively, and if you have ABS, press the brake firmly and let the system pulse the brakes for you.

question: If you are driving and the rear end of your car starts skidding to the left, you should:
options: a: Steer to the right.,b: Steer to the left.,c: Tap your brakes lightly and shift into neutral.
note: If the rear of your vehicle skids left, you should steer left—toward the same direction as the skid. This helps realign the front wheels with the direction the vehicle is sliding and allows you to regain control. At the same time, ease off the accelerator and avoid braking hard, which can make the skid worse.

question: If your vehicle begins to skid, you should:
options: a: Ease up on the gas pedal.,b: Brake as hard as possible.,c: Turn off the ignition.
note: When your vehicle begins to skid, the first step is to ease off the accelerator so the tires can regain traction. Sudden or hard braking can lock the wheels and make the skid worse, and turning off the ignition can cause loss of power steering and braking. Keep steering smoothly in the direction you want the car to go while you gently reduce speed.

question: Prior to entering a curve:
options: a: Activate your turn signal.,b: Reduce your speed.,c: Brake hard.
note: You should slow down before entering a curve so your tires can maintain good traction and you can stay in your lane. Braking hard while already in the curve can cause skidding or loss of control, especially on wet or slippery roads. Enter the curve at a safe speed, then maintain a steady speed through it.

question: What usually causes a locked wheel skid?
options: a: Braking too hard at a slow speed,b: Braking lightly at a slow speed,c: Braking too hard at a fast speed
note: A locked‑wheel skid happens when you apply the brakes so hard that one or more wheels stop turning while the car is still moving, most often at higher speeds. Braking too hard at a fast speed can overcome the tires’ traction and cause them to slide instead of roll, which leads to loss of steering control.

question: When driving on a slippery surface, such as snow or ice:
options: a: Shift to a low gear before going down steep hills.,b: Maintain traction by following other vehicles closely.,c: Pump your brakes to keep them from freezing.
note: On snow or ice, gravity will pull your vehicle downhill faster, and braking hard on a steep, slippery hill can easily cause a skid. Shifting to a lower gear before going down a steep hill lets the engine help control your speed so you can use the brakes more gently and maintain traction.

question: When stopping on snow or ice, drivers who are operating vehicles equipped with an Anti-Lock Braking System (ABS) should:
options: a: Pump the brakes.,b: Press and hold the brake pedal firmly.,c: Stay off the brakes and wait for the car to drift to a stop.
note: With ABS, you should press and hold the brake pedal firmly and let the system automatically pump the brakes for you. Do not pump the brakes yourself. Firm, continuous pressure allows ABS to rapidly apply and release braking force to prevent wheel lockup and help you maintain steering control on snow or ice.

question: You exit the freeway on a ramp that curves downhill. You should:
options: a: Slow to a safe speed before the curve.,b: Slow to the posted speed limit for the freeway.,c: Wait until you have entered the curve to begin braking.
note: You should slow to a safe speed before you enter a downhill curve. Braking while already in the curve, especially going downhill, can cause your vehicle to lose traction and skid. Enter the ramp at a speed that allows you to steer smoothly through the curve without heavy braking.

question: When the road is slippery, you should
options: a: Pump your brakes,b: Brake suddenly carefully,c: Press your brakes in slow steady strokes
note: On a slippery road without ABS, you should brake gently and gradually so the wheels keep turning and maintain traction. Pressing the brakes in slow, steady strokes helps you avoid locking the wheels and skidding. Sudden or hard braking can cause the tires to slide on wet, snowy, or icy pavement.

question: Roadways are least slippery
options: a: on bridges and in freezing temperatures,b: after it has been raining for a while,c: during the first rain after a dry spell
note: Roads are most slippery at the very beginning of a rain, especially after a dry spell, because oil and dirt have not yet been washed away. After it has been raining for a while, much of this buildup is washed off and the roadway becomes less slippery, though it can still be hazardous. Bridges, overpasses, and shaded areas can freeze before the rest of the road and may be especially slippery in freezing temperatures.

question: Hydroplaning occurs when tires ride on a thin film of water instead of on the surface of the road. To prevent hydroplaning in rainy weather, you should:
options: a: Put on your cruise control to maintain a constant speed.,b: Decrease your speed.,c: Move to the shoulder of the road as soon as it starts to rain.
note: Hydroplaning happens when your tires ride on top of water and lose contact with the road. The best way to prevent it is to slow down in wet conditions, especially when water is pooling on the road. Avoid cruise control in heavy rain so you can adjust speed quickly, and stay in your lane unless you must change for safety.

question: If a road is slippery, maintain a following distance that is:
options: a: About the same as on a dry road.,b: Farther from the car ahead than on a dry road.,c: Closer to the car ahead than on a dry road.
note: On slippery roads you need more time and distance to react and stop because your tires have less grip. Increase your following distance so you have extra space to brake gently and avoid sudden steering or braking that could cause a skid.

question: If it feels like your tires have lost contact with the surface of the road, you should:
options: a: Slow down by shifting into a lower gear.,b: Ease your foot off the gas pedal.,c: Slow down by pumping the brakes quickly and firmly.
note: If your tires lose contact with the road and you start to hydroplane, ease your foot off the accelerator and allow the vehicle to slow down gradually. Do not brake or make sudden steering movements, because that can cause a skid when the tires regain contact with the road.

question: If your vehicle starts to lose traction because of water on the road, you should:
options: a: Drive at a constant speed to gain better traction.,b: Apply the brakes firmly to prevent your vehicle from sliding.,c: Slow down gradually and not apply the brakes.
note: When your vehicle begins to hydroplane, the tires are riding on a thin layer of water and have little or no contact with the road. Any sudden input—especially hard braking—can cause a complete loss of control. You should ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually, keeping the steering wheel straight, and avoid using the brakes until your tires regain traction.

question: In inclement weather, you should:
options: a: Steer off the road.,b: Drive in a low gear.,c: Steer and brake smoothly.
note: In bad weather, roads are often wet or slippery, so sudden steering or hard braking can easily cause a skid. You should reduce your speed and make all steering, accelerating, and braking actions smooth and gentle. This helps your tires maintain traction and gives you more time to react to hazards.

question: On freezing, wet days, which of the following roadways is most likely to hide spots of ice?
options: a: Roadways near the tops of hills,b: Roadways on bridges and overpasses,c: Roadways paved with asphalt
note: On freezing, wet days, bridges and overpasses freeze before the rest of the roadway because cold air circulates above and below them. This makes them more likely to have hidden icy patches even when other parts of the road look just wet. Approach bridges and overpasses with extra caution and be prepared for reduced traction.

question: Remove all snow, frost, and ice from:
options: a: Just the windshield.,b: All windows.,c: Just the windshield and passenger window.
note: You must have a clear view in all directions to drive safely. Snow, frost, or ice on any window can block your view of other vehicles, pedestrians, or traffic signs. Before driving, completely clear all windows, as well as mirrors and lights, so you can see and be seen.

question: Roads are slippery after it first starts to rain. When the road is slippery, you should:
options: a: Avoid making turns and stops while driving at high speeds.,b: Test your tires' traction while going uphill.,c: Decrease the distance you look ahead of your vehicle.
note: When it first starts to rain, oil and dirt on the road mix with water and make the surface especially slippery. To avoid skidding, you should slow down and avoid fast turns and sudden stops. Make gradual changes in speed and direction, and increase your following distance so you have more time to brake gently.

question: Streets and highways are most slippery:
options: a: When it has been raining hard for several hours.,b: When they are clean and dry.,c: Just after it starts to rain.
note: Roads are especially slippery just after rain begins because water mixes with oil, grease, and dust that have built up on the surface. Until this layer is washed away by continued rain, tire traction is reduced and it is easier to skid, so you should slow down and drive smoothly when rain first starts.

question: Water on the road can cause a vehicle to hydroplane. Your car may hydroplane at speeds as low as:
options: a: 45 miles per hour.,b: 35 miles per hour.,c: 40 miles per hour.
note: Hydroplaning can begin at relatively low speeds if there is enough water on the road and your tires are worn or underinflated. It may start at speeds as low as about 35 mph. If you feel the steering get light or the car start to ride up on the water, ease off the accelerator and steer straight until your tires regain contact.

question: When driving under snowy or icy conditions:
options: a: It is safe to use your cruise control.,b: Make speed and directional changes more gradually than you would otherwise.,c: Drive as you would under normal conditions.
note: On snow or ice, traction is greatly reduced, so any change in speed or direction should be smooth and gradual. Sudden braking, acceleration, or sharp steering can easily cause a skid. You should slow down well in advance, increase following distance, and avoid using cruise control so you can respond quickly to changing conditions.

question: Which of the following is true about roadways on bridges and overpasses in cold, wet weather?
options: a: They tend to freeze before the rest of the road does.,b: They do not freeze because they are made of concrete.,c: They tend to freeze after the rest of the road does.
note: Bridges and overpasses lose heat from both the top and bottom, so in cold, wet weather they freeze before the rest of the road. Drivers should slow down and be especially cautious on these structures when temperatures are near freezing.

question: Which of the following roadways freeze first when wet?
options: a: Bridges and overpasses,b: Intersections,c: Tunnels
note: Because air can circulate above and below them, bridges and overpasses cool more quickly than regular roadways. When it’s wet and temperatures are near freezing, they are often the first places to form ice, so you should reduce speed and avoid sudden braking or steering on them.

question: If your car goes into water, you should
options: a: Wait for water to rush in and let it out in small breaths through your nose,b: Call the fire department immediately,c: Remove yourself from the vehicle immediately, before it starts to sink
note: If your vehicle goes into water, your priority is to get out as quickly as possible, before the car sinks. Unbuckle your seat belt, help passengers, open or break a side window, and exit immediately. Do not wait for the car to fill with water or waste time making phone calls; every second counts for getting to safety.

question: If you find that the roadway ahead of you is flooded, you should:
options: a: Slam on the brakes.,b: Not drive through the flooded area. Turn around and find another route.,c: Drive only in the center of the roadway.
note: You should never drive through a flooded roadway because you cannot accurately judge the depth or see if the road is washed out or unstable. Even shallow moving water can sweep a vehicle away. Turn around and find another route rather than risking driving through the flood.

question: What is the best advice for driving when heavy fog or dust occurs?
options: a: try not to drive until the conditions improve,b: do not drive too slowly because other drivers may hit you,c: alternate your low and high beams to improve visibility
note: In heavy fog or dust, the safest choice is to avoid driving until conditions improve because visibility can drop suddenly and severely. If you must drive, use low-beam headlights, slow down, and increase following distance, but postponing your trip is the best advice whenever possible.

question: Which of the following is true about driving in bad weather?
options: a: You should always drive at the speed limit,b: Increase your following distance,c: Use cruise control to maintain speed,d: Drive with your windows down
note: In bad weather, roads are more slippery and visibility is reduced, so you need extra time and space to react. Increasing your following distance gives you more room to stop safely if the vehicle ahead slows or stops suddenly. You should often drive below the speed limit in poor conditions, never use cruise control on slippery roads, and keep windows closed to maintain clear visibility and control.

question: You are driving and there are oncoming cars on your left and a row of parked cars on your right. You should steer:
options: a: Closer to the oncoming cars than the parked cars.,b: Closer to the parked cars than the oncoming cars.,c: A middle course between the oncoming and parked cars.
note: When you have hazards on both sides—oncoming traffic on the left and parked cars on the right—you should steer a middle course to keep as much space as possible from both dangers. Oncoming vehicles are especially dangerous because a head‑on collision is often severe, so you do not want to move closer to them. Centering your vehicle in the available lane space helps you avoid both sides safely.

question: If you can see that the roadway up ahead is covered by heavy smoke, you should:
options: a: Turn on your four-way flashers and continue.,b: Reduce your speed and use low-beam headlights.,c: Turn on your high beam headlights and continue.
note: If you must drive where there is heavy smoke or fog, you should slow down, turn on your low‑beam headlights, and be prepared to stop if visibility becomes too poor. High beams reflect off smoke or fog and create glare, making it harder to see. Hazard flashers are for stopped or very slow‑moving vehicles, not for continuing at normal speed through poor visibility.

question: Sudden wind gusts on highways:
options: a: Generally affect only the movement of large vehicles.,b: Only cause visibility problems.,c: Can cause problems for all vehicles.
note: Strong wind gusts can push any vehicle sideways and make it harder to stay in your lane. While large vehicles like trucks and vehicles towing trailers are affected more because of their size and shape, smaller cars can also be pushed or suddenly shifted. Always hold the steering wheel firmly and be prepared for sudden gusts, especially when passing large vehicles or driving in open areas.

question: If bad weather makes it difficult for you to see clearly, you should:
options: a: Speed up to get off the road quickly.,b: Drive in the lane closest to oncoming traffic.,c: Increase your following distance.
note: When you drive in fog or smoke, you should 'increase your following distance' because you may not be able to see as far ahead. This gives you more time to react if you encounter a hazard.

question: If you are riding a vehicle equipped with a lap belt and a separate shoulder belt, you are
options: a: Required to use both the lap and shoulder belt,b: Only required to use the shoulder belt,c: Only required to use the lap belt
note: If your vehicle has both a lap belt and a separate shoulder belt, you must wear both. The lap belt keeps your lower body from sliding forward, and the shoulder belt keeps your upper body from striking the steering wheel, dashboard, or windshield. Using both together provides the intended crash protection.

question: Before switching on the ignition, you should:
options: a: Buckle your safety belt.,b: Be sure all passengers have buckled their safety belts.,c: Both of the above.
note: Before you start driving, you should always buckle your own safety belt and make sure all passengers are properly buckled. The driver is responsible for ensuring that required occupants, especially children, are using seat belts or appropriate child restraints.

question: If a vehicle is equipped with airbags:
options: a: Seat belts should still be worn.,b: Seat belts do not need to be worn.,c: Seat belts should be worn behind the back.
note: Airbags are designed to work together with seat belts, not replace them. Seat belts keep you properly positioned so the airbag can protect you and prevent you from being thrown from the vehicle. You should always wear your seat belt, even in vehicles equipped with airbags.

question: If you are about to be hit from the rear, you should consider each of the following, except for:
options: a: Applying your brakes.,b: Letting go of the steering wheel.,c: Pressing your head firmly against the head restraint.
note: If you are about to be hit from the rear, you should press your head firmly against the head restraint to reduce the risk of whiplash and be ready to apply your brakes to help prevent being pushed into another vehicle. You should keep both hands on the steering wheel to maintain control; letting go of the wheel is unsafe.

question: In a vehicle equipped with airbags, the safest place for children age 12 and under to ride is in:
options: a: The front seat.,b: The back seat.,c: The bed of a pick-up truck.
note: In vehicles with airbags, children are safest in the back seat. Airbags deploy with great force and can seriously injure or kill a child in the front seat, especially smaller children or those in child seats. Children 12 and under should ride properly restrained in the rear seat whenever possible.

question: It is illegal to leave a child age six or younger unattended in a vehicle on a hot day:
options: a: Even if they are secured in a child passenger restraint system.,b: If they are supervised by a person twelve years of age or older.,c: Only if the key is in the ignition.
note: It is illegal to leave a child age 6 or younger alone in a vehicle, even if they are secured in a child restraint, because temperatures can rise quickly and other dangers exist. The only exception is when the child is supervised by a person who is at least 12 years old and remains in the vehicle with them.

question: Which child would require a child passenger restraint system?
options: a: A 9-year-old who is 4 feet 10 inches tall,b: A 10-year-old who is 5 feet 3 inches tall,c: A 7-year-old who is 4 feet 8 inches tall
note: Child passenger laws commonly require a child restraint for children under 8 years old or shorter than 4 feet 9 inches. A 7‑year‑old who is 4'8" is under 8 and under 4'9", so must be in a child passenger restraint system. The 9‑ and 10‑year‑olds listed are older than 8 and tall enough that a regular seat belt is generally allowed, provided it fits properly.

question: A highway has a posted speed limit of 65 mph. What does this mean?
options: a: You must always drive 65 mph on that highway.,b: You may drive faster only if there are no other vehicles.,c: You may drive up to 65 mph only when conditions are safe; you must slow down if conditions are not ideal.
note: A posted speed limit of 65 mph is the maximum allowed under ideal conditions, not a required speed. You must slow down below the posted limit whenever road, traffic, or weather conditions make the maximum speed unsafe. The correct idea is that you may drive up to 65 mph only when conditions are good enough to do so safely.

question: If you drive at the posted speed limit, you can be given a speeding ticket
options: a: Under no circumstances,b: If you are carrying more than one passenger,c: If road or weather conditions require a slower speed
note: You can receive a speeding ticket even while driving at or below the posted limit if that speed is unsafe for current conditions. When weather, visibility, traffic, or road surface conditions are poor, you must slow down below the posted limit.

question: The maximum posted speed limit should be driven only:
options: a: During the night.,b: During the day.,c: Under ideal conditions.
note: The maximum posted speed limit is intended for ideal conditions: good weather, dry pavement, light traffic, and clear visibility. When conditions are less than ideal, you must drive slower than the posted maximum so you can maintain control and stop safely if needed.

question: Which of the following blocks the smooth flow of traffic?
options: a: Slowing down to look at collision scene.,b: Avoiding unnecessary lane changes.,c: Using public transportation instead of your vehicle.
note: Slowing down just to look at a collision, sometimes called rubbernecking, disrupts the smooth flow of traffic and can cause sudden slowdowns or additional collisions. Safe drivers maintain a steady speed, focus on the road ahead, and avoid unnecessary distractions so traffic can keep moving smoothly.

question: You are driving on a freeway with a posted speed limit of 65 mph. Traffic is heavy and moving at 35 mph. The best speed for your vehicle is most likely:
options: a: 25 mph.,b: 35 mph.,c: 30 mph.
note: When traffic is heavy and moving well below the posted limit, you should generally travel at the speed of traffic as long as it is safe and within the legal limit. Driving much slower than surrounding traffic (such as 25 or 30 mph when others are going 35 mph) can create a hazard by forcing others to brake or change lanes suddenly.

question: If you want to pass a pedestrian who is walking along the roadway and an oncoming vehicle is approaching, you should:
options: a: Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass before you pass the pedestrian.,b: Keep driving at a steady speed. The oncoming vehicle must stop for you.,c: Honk your horn to get the pedestrian to move over.
note: When you have both an oncoming vehicle and a pedestrian in your lane on a two-lane road, you should deal with one hazard at a time. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass first, then move over safely to pass the pedestrian while giving them plenty of space. Never force the oncoming vehicle or the pedestrian into a dangerous situation.

question: What is the first thing you should do if your wheels move off the pavement?
options: a: Ease your foot off the gas pedal and brake gently,b: Pull over to the right and sound your horn to warn the other drivers,c: Pull the steering wheel back
note: If your wheels drift off the pavement, stay calm and avoid jerking the steering wheel. Firmly hold the wheel, ease your foot off the accelerator, and brake gently to slow down. Once the vehicle is under control and your speed is reduced, you can carefully steer back onto the pavement when it is safe.

question: If your accelerator becomes stuck you should
options: a: Turn off the ignition while the vehicle is moving,b: Not apply the brakes. Ease off the gas pedal and straighten the front wheels,c: Shift to neutral apply the brakes and try to drive the car safely off the road
note: If the accelerator sticks, shift to neutral right away so the engine is no longer driving the wheels. Then apply the brakes firmly and steer to the side of the road where you can stop safely. Do not turn off the ignition while moving because it can lock the steering wheel and disable power steering and brakes.

question: If your wheels drop off the roadway or pavement edge, you should:
options: a: Wait until it is safe to gently steer back onto the roadway,b: Turn back onto the roadway immediately.,c: Stop.
note: If your wheels drop off the pavement, hold the wheel firmly, ease off the gas, and slow down. When you have the car under control and it is safe, gently steer back onto the roadway. Do not jerk the wheel or turn back immediately, because that can cause you to swerve into oncoming traffic or lose control.

question: You have allowed the wheels of your vehicle to run off the edge of the pavement. What should you do first?
options: a: Turn the front wheels slightly to the left to edge the car back onto the pavement.,b: Hold the steering wheel firmly,c: Apply the brakes and turn the front wheels sharply to the left.
note: If your wheels run off the edge of the pavement, your first step is to hold the steering wheel firmly. This helps you keep control while you ease off the accelerator, slow down, and then carefully steer back onto the pavement when it is safe.

question: If your car becomes disabled while on the highway, you should:
options: a: Stop in the right lane.,b: Park with all four wheels off the traveled highway,c: Stop where you are.
note: If your car becomes disabled on a highway, you should move it completely off the traveled portion of the road if possible, with all four wheels off the roadway. Stopping in a traffic lane is extremely dangerous; use the shoulder or a safe area away from moving traffic.

question: What should you do if your cell phone rings and you do not have a hands-free device?
options: a: Answer the call and keep the conversation short.,b: Do not answer the phone and let it go to voicemail.,c: Answer the call if you are stopped at a red light.
note: If you do not have a hands‑free device and your phone rings while driving, you should not answer it. Let the call go to voicemail and keep your full attention on the road. If you must make or return a call, first pull over and stop in a safe, legal place before using the phone.

question: Distracted driving is:
options: a: Anything that causes evasive action while driving.,b: Anything that takes your attention away from driving.,c: Anything that causes you to pay more attention to driving.
note: Distracted driving is anything that takes your attention away from driving, even briefly. This includes looking at your phone, adjusting controls, eating, or focusing on passengers instead of the road. Safe drivers actively avoid these distractions so they can react quickly to traffic conditions.

question: Using a cell phone while operating a motor vehicle is considered a distraction because:
options: a: It causes the driver to be concerned about the cost of the call.,b: It occupies the driver's hands.,c: It is an activity that draws the attention of other drivers.
note: Using a handheld cell phone while driving is dangerous because it takes at least one of your hands off the steering wheel and divides your attention. When your hands and mind are occupied with a call, you are slower to react to hazards, more likely to drift in your lane, and less able to control the vehicle in an emergency.

question: What is a likely effect when you take another drug while you drink alcohol?
options: a: There are no effects unless the drug is prescription only.,b: If the drug is over‑the‑counter there are no effects.,c: The effects of the alcohol and the drug are enhanced.
note: Combining alcohol with any other drug—whether prescription, over‑the‑counter, or illegal—can greatly increase the effects of each substance. Together they can make you much more drowsy, slow your reactions, blur your vision, and impair judgment far more than either one alone, making it extremely dangerous and illegal to drive.

question: Alcohol is:
options: a: A stimulant.,b: An antihistamine.,c: A depressant.
note: Alcohol is classified as a depressant. It slows brain and nervous system activity, which reduces coordination, reaction time, and judgment. Even small amounts can affect your ability to drive safely, and higher amounts greatly increase the risk of crashes.

question: Driving under the influence of any medication which impairs your driving is permitted:
options: a: Under no circumstances.,b: If you don't feel drowsy.,c: If it is prescribed by a physician.
note: Driving under the influence of any substance that impairs you is illegal, even if it is a medication prescribed by a doctor or bought over the counter. If a drug makes you drowsy, slows your reactions, or affects your judgment, you must not drive.

question: It is legal to drive with an alcoholic beverage container that has been opened only if the container is:
options: a: Under the front seat.,b: In the glove compartment.,c: In the trunk or another area not accessible to the driver or passengers.
note: Open containers of alcohol generally must be kept in the trunk, or in another area not accessible to the driver or passengers, to prevent drinking while driving. The glove compartment or under the seat are considered accessible areas and are not acceptable places for an open container.

question: The first thing that alcohol effects is:
options: a: Vision.,b: Judgment.,c: Balance.
note: Alcohol first affects the parts of the brain that control judgment and self-control. This means you may feel more confident and take more risks, even though your driving ability is already getting worse, often before you notice changes in vision or balance.

question: Which of the following driving skills are affected by the use of alcohol and/or drugs?
options: a: Alertness and concentration.,b: Reaction time and coordination.,c: All of the above.
note: Alcohol and many drugs reduce alertness, make it harder to concentrate, slow your reaction time, and affect your coordination. Because all of these skills are needed for safe driving, any impairment greatly increases your risk of a crash.

question: Which of the following substances can affect the ability to drive?
options: a: Tranquilizers,b: Cough syrups and cold tablets containing codeine or antihistamines.,c: All of the above.
note: Many substances can impair driving, including tranquilizers and common cough or cold medicines that contain codeine or antihistamines. These drugs can cause drowsiness, slower reactions, and poor judgment. Driving under the influence of any drug that affects your ability to drive safely is illegal, whether it is prescription, over‑the‑counter, or illegal.

question: While in a motor vehicle on a highway, it is:
options: a: Illegal to either drink from or possess open containers of alcohol.,b: Legal to drink alcohol if you're not driving.,c: Legal to drink alcohol if you're driving but not drunk.
note: Open‑container laws generally make it illegal to drink alcohol or possess an open container of alcohol in the passenger area of a motor vehicle on a public road, whether you are the driver or a passenger. Alcohol in an open container must be in a trunk or other area not normally occupied by people. You may not legally drink in the vehicle just because you are not the one driving.

question: If you are arrested for drunk driving and refuse to submit to a chemical test of the alcohol content of your blood
options: a: Your driving privilege will be withdrawn,b: You will receive an additional fine,c: You will not be allowed to post bail
note: Under implied‑consent laws, by driving you agree to take a chemical test (breath, blood, or sometimes urine) if lawfully arrested for DUI. If you refuse the test, the DMV will automatically suspend or revoke your driving privilege, often for at least one year, even if you are not later convicted in court.

question: Your BAC depends on
options: a: How much time passes between drinks,b: How much alcohol you drink,c: All of the above
note: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) is affected by how much alcohol you drink and how quickly you drink it. The body can only process a certain amount of alcohol per hour, so drinking more in a short time raises BAC. Body weight and other factors also matter, but among the listed choices, both the amount of alcohol and the time between drinks are key influences.

question: BAC is
options: a: The acronym for Beer Accumulation,b: The number of ounces of alcohol in your blood,c: The percentage of alcohol in your blood
